This policy meets: 295.2030(b)(1), terms of occupancy, including resident responsibilities and obligations; 295.2030(b)(2), the amount and purpose of any fee, charge and deposit, including any fee or charge for days a resident is absent; 295.2030(b)(3), the establishment's policy for refunding fees, charges or deposits; 295.2030(b)(4), the establishment's responsibility to give at least 30 days' written notice before any change in a fee or charge, except that 30 days' notice of an increase is not required for a resident whose service needs change as documented in the service plan; and 295.2030(b)(5), the establishment's policy on notifying a relative or other individual in an emergency, significant change in the resident's condition, or termination of residency. A copy of the signed contract goes to the resident or representative. No fee, charge or deposit will be collected unless it is stated in the contract or its signed amendment.

definitions.definition: Any money the establishment requires from a resident, including the base rate, extra-service charges, move-in or community fees, security or other deposits, and any charge for days of absence.
Days when the resident is away from the establishment (for example, hospitalization or family visit) while the unit remains reserved.
The relative, representative or other individual the resident names in the contract or record to be notified (see RTS-03).
A change in the resident's physical, cognitive, mental or functional status that is expected to continue and that requires a reassessment or changes to the service plan (see CARE-05).

procedures: Occupancy terms (b)(1): The contract states the terms of occupancy: unit assignment, move-in date, house rules, the resident's responsibilities (for example, paying fees on time, following the service plan and safety rules, and cooperating with the assessment) and the establishment's obligations. The administrator reviews these terms with the resident at signing.

Fee disclosure (b)(2): The contract and its attached fee schedule list the amount and purpose of each fee, charge and deposit, including the base rate, charges for extra services, and any charge for days the resident is absent. If we do not charge for absences, the contract says so. The business office uses only the fee schedule in the contract for billing.
Pre-signing review: Before signature, admissions staff walk through all charges and deposits with the resident and representative and give them the written fee schedule to keep.
Deposit handling: The business office issues a written receipt for every deposit. Deposits are recorded and held under CON-03 and are not mixed with operating funds.

Refund policy (b)(3): The contract states when and how each fee, charge and deposit is refunded, including refunds after a move-out, death, transfer or termination: the refund amount, any proration of fees, any amounts that may be deducted, and the deadline of [NUMBER] days after the resident leaves or the contract ends. The business office follows this policy in every case.

Refund processing: Within the contract deadline, the business office issues the refund to the resident or the representative or estate, with an itemized statement of any deductions. A second person (administrator or designee) reviews each refund before payment. Copies go in the resident's financial file.

Fee-change notice (b)(4): Before any change in a fee or charge takes effect, the administrator gives the resident and representative written notice at least 30 days in advance. The notice states the old amount, new amount, reason, and effective date. Delivery is documented on the Fee-Change Notice Log with date, method and recipient.

Service-need exception (b)(4): When a fee changes only because the resident's service needs have changed, the 30-day notice is not required. The care/nurse designee must first document the change in the service plan (CARE-01). The administrator gives the resident and representative written notice of the new charge as soon as the service plan is updated and refers to the service plan change. The administrator never uses this exception for general rate increases.
Amendments: Fee changes for existing residents that alter the contract terms are put in writing and signed by both parties (CON-01). The signed amendment is filed in the resident's record.

Emergency notification (b)(5): The contract states that we will notify the designated person of an emergency, a significant change in the resident's condition, or the termination of residency. At admission, admissions staff record the name, relationship, phone numbers and the preferred order of contact for each designated person, and note any resident preferences about whom not to notify.

Emergency response: In a medical emergency, staff call 911 first and begin care within their training and scope. As soon as the resident is safe, the nurse designee or shift supervisor notifies the designated person by phone. If no one is reached, staff retry at least every [NUMBER] minutes and try each alternate contact, and record each attempt (CARE-05).

Significant change notification: When a change of condition is identified, the nurse designee informs the physician and then the designated person on the same day, or as soon as the resident's wishes and safety allow, and documents the call.
Termination notification: When termination of residency is initiated, the administrator notifies the resident and designated person in writing as set out in TERM-01 and documents it.
Contract copy: Admissions staff give a copy of the signed contract and all attachments to the resident or representative at signing and record the date. The signed original stays on the premises.

Billing audit: Each month, the business office compares a sample of billing statements with the contract fee schedule and fee-change notices. The administrator reviews exceptions, corrects billing errors and reimburses the resident for any overcharge within [NUMBER] days.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the fee schedule and refund policy, signs fee-change notices, and reviews refunds and billing audits.
Bills according to the contract, issues receipts and refunds, keeps the Fee-Change Notice Log, and performs the monthly billing audit.
Review terms with residents, record designated persons, and give contract copies.
Document service plan changes and make emergency and change-in-condition notifications.

documentation: Signed contract, fee schedule and amendments
Deposit receipts and refund statements with reviewer sign-off
Fee-Change Notice Log and copies of notices
Service plan documentation supporting any service-need fee change
Designated person contact record
Notification attempt notes in the resident record
Monthly billing audit results

policies.category: Subpart B – Policies: § 295.2030 Establishment Contracts
policies.title: Resident Funds and Personal Property
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; administrator, business office, all staff who handle resident money or belongings
policies.purpose: To protect resident money and belongings from loss, misuse or exploitation, and to make sure deposits and refunds are handled according to the contract.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not take control of a resident's money without the resident's (or representative's) written authorization. Any resident funds handled by staff are held on a separate, itemized ledger for each resident and never commingled with operating funds. Deposits and refunds are handled in line with the refund policy stated in the resident's contract (CON-01 and CON-02, 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2030), and billing must match the contract fee schedule. Staff may not borrow from, sell to, accept gifts of value from, or be named as beneficiaries by residents. Any suspected misuse is reported under RTS-02.

definitions.definition: Money or negotiable items belonging to a resident that the establishment holds or manages at the resident's request, other than fees paid to the establishment.
Money paid to the establishment under the contract and held until it is applied or refunded.
A separate record for each resident showing every deposit, withdrawal and balance, with date, amount, purpose and signatures.
Furniture, clothing, jewelry, devices and other items the resident brings to or acquires while in the establishment.

procedures: Default practice: Staff encourage residents to manage their own money. The establishment does not hold resident funds unless the resident or representative requests it in writing.

Written authorization: Before holding any funds, the business office obtains a signed authorization stating the amount or type of funds, the purpose, who may deposit or withdraw, and that the resident or representative may withdraw at any time. The authorization is filed in the resident's financial record.

Separate account and ledger: The business office keeps resident funds in a [SEPARATE BANK ACCOUNT / LOCKED CASH BOX] used only for resident funds. It maintains a separate itemized ledger for each resident. Resident funds are never mixed with operating funds or used for establishment expenses.

Transactions: Each deposit and withdrawal is made by [BUSINESS OFFICE DESIGNEE], who writes a receipt. The resident or representative signs the ledger for each withdrawal. A second staff member witnesses and signs any cash transaction over [AMOUNT].
Statements: The business office gives the resident or representative an itemized statement of the account at least quarterly and on request within [NUMBER] business days.

Monthly reconciliation: The administrator or a designee who does not handle the funds reconciles the ledger balances to the account or cash on hand every month and signs the reconciliation. Discrepancies are investigated at once and reported to the administrator the same day.

Contract deposits: Deposits required by the contract are receipted, recorded, and held as the contract states. They are applied or refunded only under the contract's refund policy (CON-02), with an itemized statement of any deductions.
Fee consistency: The business office bills only the amounts in the contract fee schedule or a signed amendment, and reviews billing monthly (CON-02).

Personal property inventory: At admission, staff and the resident or representative list the resident's personal property on a dated inventory form, which both sign. Staff update the inventory when items are added or removed.

Valuables: Staff encourage residents to keep valuables out of the establishment or in a locked place in their unit. If we hold valuables for safekeeping, they are listed on the inventory, receipted and kept locked, with access limited to [DESIGNEE].

Loss reports: When a resident or family reports lost or missing property or money, staff take a written report the same day, search the area, and notify the administrator. The administrator investigates within [NUMBER] days, tells the resident or representative the outcome in writing, and reports suspected theft or exploitation under RTS-02.

Staff prohibitions: Staff may not borrow money or property from residents, use a resident's accounts or cards, serve as the resident's agent for financial matters unless permitted by law and authorized in writing and approved by the administrator, or accept gifts beyond token value (PER-08).

Move-out and death: At discharge, transfer or death, staff reconcile the ledger and inventory within [NUMBER] days and return funds and property to the resident, representative or the estate, with signed receipts (CLO-01 if a closure applies).
Training: The administrator trains staff who handle money or property on this policy at orientation and annually (PER-06).
Review: The Quality Improvement committee reviews reconciliations, loss reports and refunds quarterly (QI-01).

responsibilities.duty: Oversees this policy, reviews reconciliations, investigates losses, and reports suspected exploitation.
Holds funds, keeps ledgers, issues receipts and statements, and processes deposits and refunds.

responsibilities.role: Independent reviewer (designee who does not handle funds)
responsibilities.duty: Performs the monthly reconciliation.
Follow the staff prohibitions, take loss reports, and report concerns.

documentation: Written authorizations for resident funds
Separate itemized ledger for each resident and receipts
Quarterly resident statements
Monthly reconciliation signed by the reviewer
Personal property inventories with updates
Loss reports and investigation findings
Deposit and refund statements

policies.category: Subpart B – Policies: § 295.2040 Disaster Preparedness
policies.title: Written Disaster Plan: Relocation, Severe Weather and Power Outages
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; administrator, all staff, maintenance, nursing/care staff
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] has a written disaster plan that protects every person in the building, addresses residents' physical and cognitive needs, and covers temporary relocation, tornado and severe thunderstorm warnings, and power outages.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written disaster plan under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2040(b)(1) (Part 295, C16). This policy meets 295.2040(b)(1): the plan protects all persons in the event of disasters by keeping persons in place, evacuating them to areas of refuge, and evacuating them from the building when necessary. The plan addresses the physical and cognitive needs of residents and includes special staff response and the procedures needed to ensure each resident's safety. The plan is amended or revised whenever a resident with unusual needs is admitted. This policy also meets 295.2040(b)(1)(A), by providing for the temporary relocation of residents for any disaster requiring relocation; 295.2040(b)(1)(B), by providing for the movement of residents to safe locations within the establishment when the National Weather Service issues a tornado warning or severe thunderstorm warning; and 295.2040(b)(1)(E), by addressing power outages. Temperature extremes under 295.2040(b)(1)(C) and (D) are covered in DIS-02, and drills in DIS-03. If we operate a special dementia program, the plan also includes emergency procedures and staffing patterns for that program, and wandering and evacuation safety under 210 ILCS 9/150 (C5).

definitions.term: Shelter in place (keeping persons in place)
definitions.definition: Keeping residents inside the building in their current location or a safer interior location when that is the safest option.
A designated location in the building, such as an interior hallway or room, to which residents are moved for protection from a hazard.
Moving residents out of the building, or out of an affected area, when it is unsafe to remain.
Alerts issued by the National Weather Service that a tornado or severe thunderstorm is occurring or imminent in the area.

A resident whose mobility, cognition, equipment, medical or behavioral needs would require special staff response in a disaster (e.g., bed-bound, oxygen- or power-dependent, a dementia resident at risk of wandering).

procedures: Plan ownership: The administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) owns the written disaster plan. The plan is kept in a binder at the main desk and on each shift supervisor's desk, and an offsite copy is kept at [LOCATION].

Hazard assessment: The administrator reviews the plan at least annually and after any real event or drill. The review covers local hazards (tornado, severe thunderstorm, flood, winter storm, extreme heat or cold, fire, utility failure, hazardous material release, and others), the building's layout, and the resident population. It is documented in the plan revision log.

Keep in place, refuge and evacuation: The plan states for each hazard whether to keep persons in place, move them to areas of refuge, or evacuate the building, who gives the order (the administrator or, if unavailable, the shift supervisor), and how the decision is communicated. Floor plans in the plan mark the areas of refuge and exits.

Resident needs roster: The nurse/care designee keeps a current roster that lists each resident's mobility level, cognitive status, equipment, medications, diet, and evacuation assistance needed, with the number of staff required. The roster is updated at admission, at a change in condition, and at least monthly, and a copy goes in the disaster binder and the evacuation go-kit.

Admission of residents with unusual needs: Before admitting a resident with unusual needs, the administrator and nurse/care designee decide what special staff response is needed and revise the disaster plan. The revision is dated and signed, and staff on all shifts are briefed on it before or at the time of the resident's move-in (RES-01, CARE-01).

Temporary relocation (A): The plan names at least [NUMBER] relocation sites, such as [SITE NAME AND ADDRESS], with a written agreement or confirmed contact for each, for any disaster that requires relocation. It lists the transportation arrangements ([TRANSPORT PROVIDER]), the route, and who accompanies residents. The administrator verifies the agreements and contact numbers at least annually.

Relocation procedure: On a decision to relocate, the shift supervisor assigns staff to account for every resident using the roster, prepare the go-kit (current roster, medications, MARs, diet information, emergency contact numbers, advance directives, supplies), and move residents as the plan directs. Charge nurse or designee tracks each resident's whereabouts on a log until return.

Notification during relocation: The administrator or designee notifies IDPH, each resident's representative and designated person (CON-02), physicians and service providers (hospice, home health) that relocation has occurred and where residents are. Notifications are logged.

Tornado and severe thunderstorm warnings (B): The plan identifies safe locations inside the building for each wing or floor, away from windows and exterior glass. Staff monitor National Weather Service alerts through [WEATHER RADIO / ALERT APP / OTHER SOURCE]. When a tornado warning or severe thunderstorm warning is issued for our area, the shift supervisor immediately announces it and directs staff to move residents to the designated safe locations. Doors to rooms are closed and residents are kept away from windows.

Weather response details: Staff bring the resident roster and flashlights, assist residents who cannot walk, and stay with residents who may be frightened or may wander. Staff do not release residents from safe locations until the warning has expired or the shift supervisor says it is safe. The supervisor then checks the building for damage and reports the all-clear.

Power outages (E): The plan states who is called first ([MAINTENANCE / UTILITY CONTACT] and the administrator), the location of flashlights and batteries, and the backup power available ([GENERATOR DESCRIPTION OR NONE]). It describes how staff protect residents who depend on electrical equipment (oxygen concentrators, powered beds and mattresses, nebulizers), how medications requiring refrigeration are protected, how meals, water and hygiene are provided, and when an outage requires relocation.

Outage escalation: Staff check on residents in rooms at least every [NUMBER] minutes during an outage. The shift supervisor records indoor temperature readings as set out in DIS-02. The administrator decides on relocation if the outage threatens residents' safety or if the temperature thresholds in DIS-02 are met.

Dementia program: If we operate a special dementia program, the plan includes emergency procedures and staffing patterns for that program, wandering and evacuation safety measures (such as additional staff for escorting, headcounts at areas of refuge, and photographs for each resident), and communication with family (210 ILCS 9/150, C5; CARE-04, SAF-01).
Staff training: All new staff are trained on the plan during orientation, and all staff are retrained at least annually and whenever the plan is revised (PER-06). Training attendance is recorded.
Drills: The plan is tested through the drills in DIS-03, and the written evaluations are used to improve it.
After any real event, the administrator completes a written review within [NUMBER] days, revises the plan as needed, and reports any serious incident to IDPH under INC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Owns, reviews and revises the plan; decides on relocation and evacuation; maintains relocation agreements; and notifies IDPH.
Maintains the resident needs roster and go-kit, advises on special staff response, and tracks residents during any relocation.
Directs staff response on the shift, announces weather warnings, and keeps logs.
Maintains backup power, emergency lighting and supplies, and checks the building after an event.
Know their roles in the plan and carry them out.

documentation: Written disaster plan with revision log and dates
Annual hazard assessment
Resident needs roster and evacuation go-kit contents list
Relocation site agreements and transportation arrangements
Revisions made for residents with unusual needs
Weather alert monitoring log and event logs
Staff training records
After-event review reports

policies.category: Subpart B – Policies: § 295.2040 Disaster Preparedness
policies.title: Heat, Cold and Temperature Extremes
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; administrator, maintenance, nursing/care staff, all staff
policies.purpose: To protect residents from the dangers of cold and heat by requiring monitoring of indoor temperatures, temporary relocation when bedrooms get too cold, and added protective measures when the heat index inside the building is too high.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows the temperature requirements of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2040(b)(1) (Part 295, C16). This policy meets 295.2040(b)(1)(C): we will temporarily relocate residents any time the temperature in residents' bedrooms falls below 55°F for 12 hours or more because of a mechanical problem or loss of power. This policy meets 295.2040(b)(1)(D): we will provide for the health, safety, welfare and comfort of all residents when the heat index/apparent temperature (Table A of Part 295, in the Subpart I appendices) inside living, dining, activities or sleeping areas exceeds 80°F. Staff monitor and log indoor temperatures and, in hot weather, the heat index, every day. The relocation procedures of DIS-01 apply when relocation is needed. The action levels below that are earlier than the regulatory thresholds are the establishment's own safety triggers.

definitions.definition: The combined effect of air temperature and humidity, determined from Table A of Part 295 using the indoor temperature and relative humidity readings.
The heat index table in the Subpart I appendices of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295, kept in the temperature log binder.
Moving residents to a safe, comfortably heated location, within or outside the building, until normal temperatures are restored.

A resident at higher risk from heat or cold, such as one who is frail, has a chronic condition, takes medications affecting heat tolerance or fluid balance, has dementia, or cannot communicate discomfort.

procedures: Equipment: Maintenance keeps in the building [NUMBER] calibrated thermometers with hygrometers (relative humidity) placed in [LOCATIONS: living area, dining area, activity area, and sample resident bedrooms on each wing]. Maintenance checks calibration every [NUMBER] months and replaces faulty units.

Daily monitoring: Each day, the designated staff member reads the indoor temperatures in the living, dining and activity areas and in sample bedrooms at [TIMES, e.g., 7:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m.], and records them with the time, location and initials on the Temperature and Heat Index Log.

Hot weather monitoring: When the outdoor forecast is 80°F or above, or when the indoor reading is at or above [75°F], staff also record the relative humidity and determine the heat index from Table A at each reading. Readings are taken at least every [NUMBER] hours during the day and evening.

Heat response (D): When the heat index inside living, dining, activities or sleeping areas exceeds 80°F, the shift supervisor immediately notifies the administrator and starts the heat protocol. The supervisor records the start time on the log.

Heat protocol steps: Staff (a) turn on or adjust air conditioning and fans and close blinds and curtains on sun-exposed windows; (b) move residents to the coolest areas of the building; (c) offer cool fluids to each resident at least every [NUMBER] hour(s), within any physician-ordered fluid limits; (d) encourage light clothing and bedding; (e) check each heat-vulnerable resident at least every [NUMBER] minutes for signs of heat illness such as flushed or dry skin, confusion, dizziness, headache, nausea, rapid pulse or reduced urine; (f) schedule activities during cooler hours and limit exertion and outdoor time; and (g) record actions taken on the log.

Heat illness: If a resident shows signs of heat illness, staff move the resident to a cool place, begin cooling measures, notify the nurse/care designee, and call 911 for severe symptoms. The physician and representative are notified under CARE-05.

Persistent heat: If the heat index remains above 80°F despite these measures for more than [NUMBER] hours, or if air conditioning fails, the administrator decides on moving residents to a cooler location under the relocation procedures in DIS-01, and notifies IDPH as required by INC-01.

Cold monitoring: In cold weather, or whenever there is a heating or power problem, staff check bedroom temperatures in each wing at least every [NUMBER] hours and record them on the log. An internal alert applies at [60°F]: staff notify maintenance and the administrator and start corrective measures such as repairs, supplemental safe heat sources approved by the administrator, extra blankets and warm clothing.

Cold relocation (C): If the temperature in residents' bedrooms falls below 55°F because of a mechanical problem or loss of power, the shift supervisor notifies the administrator at once and records the time the temperature fell below 55°F. If the temperature stays below 55°F for 12 hours or more, the administrator temporarily relocates the affected residents to a safe, adequately heated location under DIS-01. The administrator plans for relocation earlier than the 12-hour mark when forecasts show the problem will not be fixed in time.

Relocation execution: Staff use the resident needs roster, move residents with their medications and records, notify representatives and physicians (CON-02), and log each resident's location. Residents return only after the heating is repaired and temperatures are back in a safe range, confirmed and recorded by maintenance.

Repairs: Maintenance calls the heating, cooling or utility service provider immediately for any failure, keeps contact numbers in the disaster binder, and documents the time called, time repaired and cause.
Staff training: Staff are trained at orientation and annually on how to take the readings, use Table A, recognize heat illness and hypothermia, and take the actions in this policy (PER-06).
Review: The administrator reviews the logs weekly during hot and cold seasons, and the Quality Improvement committee reviews each event and any trend in building temperatures (QI-01, PP-02).

responsibilities.duty: Decides on relocation and protective measures, notifies IDPH when required, and reviews logs.
Maintains thermometers, heating and cooling equipment and backup power, and responds to failures.
Ensures daily readings, starts the heat and cold protocols and notifies the administrator.
Identifies heat-vulnerable residents, monitors residents for heat illness and hypothermia, and notifies physicians.
Take readings, offer fluids, check on residents and report problems promptly.

documentation: Temperature and Heat Index Log with readings, heat index values and actions
Copy of Table A (Part 295 Subpart I appendices) in the log binder
Thermometer calibration records
Relocation records and resident location logs
Heating and cooling repair records
Heat illness and hypothermia incident notes
Training records and weekly administrator review sign-off

policies.category: Subpart B – Policies: § 295.2040 Disaster Preparedness
policies.title: Emergency Drills and Written Drill Evaluations
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] practices its emergency procedures, evaluates every drill in writing, gives each evaluation to the establishment manager, and keeps the evaluation for one year so staff are prepared and the records are ready for IDPH survey.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] conducts the emergency drills required by its written Disaster Plan (DIS-01) and by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2040. A written evaluation is prepared for each drill, submitted to the establishment manager, and maintained for one year from the date of the drill. This policy meets 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2040(h): a written evaluation of each drill is submitted to the establishment manager and maintained for one year from the date of the drill. Drill types and frequencies follow the current text of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2040 and the schedule in the Disaster Plan. The Administrator confirms them against the current rule text before this manual is adopted and at each annual policy review (GOV-01). The same drill records are used for IDPH survey review and for the Quality Improvement Program (QI-01).

definitions.definition: A planned practice of an emergency procedure in the Disaster Plan, such as evacuation or relocation, sheltering from severe weather, or response to a power outage, carried out with on-duty staff and, where appropriate, residents.
The written review of a drill, completed by the person who conducted or observed it and submitted to the establishment manager.
The full-time manager/director of [AGENCY NAME], currently [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

procedures: The Administrator keeps an annual drill calendar listing each required drill type, the frequency required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2040 and the Disaster Plan (DIS-01), and the assigned staff lead. The calendar is reviewed each January and whenever the Disaster Plan changes.

The Administrator checks the drill types and frequencies in the calendar against the current rule text before adoption of this manual and at each annual policy review. Any difference is corrected within 30 days and recorded in the policy review log.
The drill lead schedules each drill so that, over the year, drills occur on different shifts, including overnight shifts, and on different days, so every employee takes part in drills.
Before each drill, the drill lead briefs participating staff on the scenario, the roles each person has, and the safety limits. Residents are never placed at risk for the sake of a drill.

The drill lead decides how residents take part, based on each resident's service plan and mobility, including residents who cannot move to safety without help (see PER-01). Staff help residents who need it, and no resident is forced to take part.
During the drill, the lead or a designated observer records the date, start and end times, shift, drill type and scenario, staff on duty and their roles, residents who took part, and any problem.

The drill lead completes a written drill evaluation on the Drill Evaluation Form within 3 calendar days after the drill. The evaluation records what happened, how well staff carried out their assigned roles, time to complete the key actions, delays or hazards found, whether equipment worked (for example alarms, flashlights, evacuation aids, communication tools), and corrective actions needed. It also includes any further content required by the current text of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2040.
The drill lead signs and dates the evaluation and submits it to the establishment manager, and the manager records the date received. This meets 295.2040(h).
Within 7 calendar days after receipt, the Administrator reviews the evaluation, assigns each corrective action to a named person with a due date, and documents completion.
The Administrator reviews problems from the drill with all staff, including those on other shifts, and updates the Disaster Plan, staff training (PER-06), or equipment as needed.
Corrective action is re-checked at the next drill. If the same problem occurs again, the Administrator escalates it to the Quality Improvement Committee (QI-01).

Drill evaluations are filed in the Disaster Preparedness binder, by date, and kept for at least one year from the date of each drill. They are not discarded early. Evaluations tied to a survey citation or investigation are held until the matter is resolved.
Records are kept at the establishment and produced on request to IDPH surveyors. The Administrator tests retrieval of the prior 12 months of evaluations at least once a year.

Fire drills and evacuation timing in the Life Safety Code program (PP-03) use the same evaluation form. Each is filed according to this policy and, if a separate fire safety retention period applies, the longer period is used.

responsibilities.duty: Keeps the drill calendar, receives and reviews every written drill evaluation, assigns and verifies corrective action, ensures one-year retention, and produces records for surveyors.
Conducts the drill, completes the written evaluation within 3 calendar days, and submits it to the establishment manager.
Participate in drills, perform assigned roles, and report equipment or procedural problems.
Reviews drill trends and repeated problems quarterly.

documentation: Annual drill calendar
Drill Evaluation Form for each drill, submitted to the establishment manager with date-received notation
Corrective action log with due dates and completion dates
Drill participation sign-in sheets
Policy review log recording the rule-text check of drill frequencies

policies.category: Subpart B – Policies: § 295.2050 Incident and Accident Reporting
policies.title: Serious Incident and Accident Reporting to IDPH
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment
policies.purpose: To make sure every serious incident or accident involving a resident is identified, reported to the IDPH Division of Assisted Living within 24 hours, communicated to the resident's representative or designated relative, and documented and retained.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports to the Illinois Department of Public Health any serious incident or accident. This policy meets 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2050(a): "serious" means any incident or accident that causes physical or emotional harm or injury to a resident, and a change in a resident's condition due to health or medical decline is not a reportable incident or accident. This policy meets 295.2050(b): the report is made to the IDPH Division of Assisted Living by email at DPH.LTCAL@illinois.gov, or as the Department requests, within 24 hours after the incident or accident. This policy meets 295.2050(c): a copy of the report is maintained for one year after the date of the incident or accident. The resident's representative or designated relative is also notified under the notification policy in the resident's contract (CON-02). Failure to meet reporting and other licensing requirements may result in civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation, with each day a separate violation (210 ILCS 9/135).

definitions.definition: Any incident or accident that causes physical or emotional harm or injury to a resident (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2050(a)). Examples include a fall with injury, a medication error that causes harm, an assault or altercation between residents, an elopement that results in harm, a burn, choking, or an event that causes emotional harm.

definitions.term: Change in condition due to health or medical decline
definitions.definition: A resident's gradual or sudden health decline that is not the result of an incident or accident. It is not reportable under this policy but is handled under CARE-05.
The division of IDPH that licenses and surveys assisted living and shared housing establishments.
The written internal form used by [AGENCY NAME] to record any incident or accident, whether or not it is reportable to IDPH.

procedures: Any employee who witnesses or discovers an incident or accident involving a resident first makes sure the resident is safe, gives or summons emergency help (call 911 when needed), and notifies the staff member in charge immediately.
The staff member in charge reports the event to the Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or the on-call manager at [PHONE] as soon as the resident is safe, at any hour.

The employee with direct knowledge completes an Incident Report before the end of the shift. It records date, time, location, residents and staff involved, a factual description, injuries or harm observed, immediate actions, witnesses, and notifications made.

The Administrator or on-call manager decides within 2 hours of notice whether the event is "serious" by asking: did it cause physical or emotional harm or injury to a resident? If there is any doubt, treat the event as reportable and report it.

An event that is only a change in condition from health or medical decline, with no incident or accident, is not reported under this policy. It is handled under CARE-05 (physician notification and transfer). If the change may have been caused by an incident, accident, neglect or abuse, it is reviewed as a possible reportable event.
If the event involves suspected abuse, neglect or financial exploitation, the Administrator follows RTS-02 for the separate mandated reporting in addition to this policy.

For a reportable event, the Administrator or designee emails the report to the IDPH Division of Assisted Living at DPH.LTCAL@illinois.gov, or by whatever other method the Department requests, no later than 24 hours after the incident or accident. The 24 hours run from the time of the incident, not from the time of discovery of the report, so staff do not delay.

The report states the establishment name and license information, the date and time of the event, the resident's identifying information, a short factual description, the harm or injury, immediate action taken, medical treatment, and a contact person. It is limited to the information needed to describe the event and sent in a way that protects resident privacy (RTS-05).
If the 24-hour deadline falls on a weekend or holiday, the on-call manager sends the report on time. Weekends and holidays do not extend the deadline.
The Administrator saves the sent email or confirmation with its date and time stamp as proof of timely reporting and records the time of the report on the Incident Report.

The Administrator or designee notifies the resident's representative or designated relative, following the notification policy in the contract (CON-02). The notification is made promptly after the resident is stable and is documented with date, time, person contacted and person who made the call.
The nurse or other staff member responsible for care updates the resident's record, and the Service Plan is reviewed and revised if needed (CARE-01). Fall events are also reviewed under CARE-06.
The Administrator completes an internal review within 5 working days, identifies the root cause and preventive actions, assigns follow-up, and answers any further questions from IDPH.

Incident Reports and the IDPH report are filed in a confidential incident file, not in the resident's chart alone. A copy of the report is maintained for at least one year after the date of the incident or accident. Reports connected to a pending investigation, claim or survey citation are held until the matter ends.

The Administrator reviews all incidents and reports at least monthly for patterns, such as repeated falls, locations, shifts or staff involved, and presents them to the Quality Improvement Committee quarterly (QI-01).
All staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually (PER-06), including the difference between a reportable incident and a medical decline.

responsibilities.duty: Determines reportability, sends or oversees the IDPH report within 24 hours, ensures family/representative notification, completes review, and ensures one-year retention.
Performs the Administrator's duties when the Administrator is unavailable, including meeting the 24-hour deadline.
Secures resident safety, notifies the manager immediately, and ensures an Incident Report is written.
Report any incident or accident immediately and complete the Incident Report accurately.
Reviews incident trends and monitors preventive action.

documentation: Incident Report for each incident or accident
Copy of the report sent to IDPH (DPH.LTCAL@illinois.gov) with date/time of transmission, kept for at least one year after the date of the incident or accident
Representative or designated relative notification log
Internal incident review and corrective action record
Monthly incident log and quarterly QI summary

policies.category: Subpart B – Policies: § 295.2060 Quality Improvement Program
policies.title: Quality Improvement Program
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment
policies.purpose: To establish and maintain an ongoing, data-driven quality improvement program centered on resident satisfaction, with a system to detect and resolve problems quickly, and to provide the proof of an ongoing program that is required with the license application.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains an effective Quality Improvement (QI) program. This policy meets 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2060(a): the program covers oversight and monitoring, resident satisfaction, and ongoing quality improvement and implementation of any plan for improved quality services, and the process benchmarks performance, is customer centered, is data driven, and focuses on resident satisfaction. This policy meets 295.2060(b): a system is in place to facilitate the detection of issues and problems, to expedite the implementation of action, and to resolve problems. This policy and the records it produces are the proof of an ongoing quality improvement program submitted with the license application under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.500(a)(8).

definitions.definition: The group led by the Administrator that reviews data, sets goals, and oversees improvement plans. Members include the Administrator, the nurse or care lead, a direct care staff representative, the dining/food service lead, the maintenance lead, and, when willing, a resident or resident representative.

A measure of the establishment's performance compared with its own prior results and with outside reference points, such as targets set by the Governing Body, survey results, or published industry data.
The written annual plan listing priority areas, measures, targets, responsible persons and timelines.
A tracked measure such as falls, medication errors, incident reports, grievances, resident satisfaction scores, staff turnover, and response times.

procedures: The Governing Body and Administrator appoint the QI Committee in writing and review its membership each year (GOV-01).

The QI Committee meets at least quarterly, and more often when a serious problem is found. The Administrator prepares an agenda and the Committee secretary takes written minutes for each meeting, listing attendees, data reviewed, decisions, action items, responsible persons and due dates.

By the first quarter of each year, the Committee adopts a written QI Plan that covers three areas: (a) oversight and monitoring of services and operations, (b) resident satisfaction, and (c) ongoing quality improvement, including implementation of any improvement plan.

The QI Plan names the quality indicators to track. At minimum these include incidents and accidents (INC-01), falls and skin integrity (CARE-06), medication errors and variances (MED-01), grievances and complaints (RTS-04), resident satisfaction results, drill evaluation findings (DIS-03), infection events (CARE-03), staffing and personnel schedule sufficiency (PER-01), and survey results (GOV-02).

For each indicator the QI Plan sets a measurable target and a benchmark, using the establishment's own baseline and any outside reference chosen by the Governing Body, so performance is benchmarked as required by 295.2060(a).
Staff collect the data monthly. The Administrator compiles it on the QI Dashboard, with the previous year's results for comparison.

Resident satisfaction is measured at least annually with a written survey given to every resident, offered in the resident's language and with help for residents who need it (RTS-06). Representatives and families are surveyed as well. Surveys may be anonymous. Results are tabulated by the Administrator within 30 days.
Resident Council or informal resident input, when held, and day-to-day comments logged by staff are also reviewed as customer-centered input.

The detection system works as follows. Staff report concerns to the Administrator on the same shift using the Concern Log. Incident reports, grievances, medication variances and maintenance requests are all entered in the log or cross-referenced to it. The Administrator reviews the log each business day.

To expedite action, the Administrator assigns a responsible person and a due date within 2 business days for any problem logged. Problems affecting resident health or safety are addressed immediately, and the Administrator is notified at once.

The Administrator or designee resolves each problem, records the action taken, and follows up with the resident or person who raised the concern. The problem is closed only when the Administrator confirms that the fix worked.

For any indicator that misses its target, or any trend or repeated problem, the Committee writes a performance improvement plan stating the problem, root cause, actions, person responsible, timeline and how success will be measured. The plan is implemented and re-measured the next quarter.
The Administrator reports QI results and plans to the Governing Body at least twice a year and shares a summary of improvements with residents and staff.
Staff are trained on the QI program at orientation (PER-06) and are encouraged to report problems without fear of retaliation.

The Administrator keeps QI Plans, minutes, dashboards, survey results, improvement plans and Concern Logs in a QI binder for at least 3 years so that the history of an ongoing program is available to IDPH surveyors. These records stay available on site.

A copy of this policy and the current QI Plan and recent minutes are included in the license application packet as proof of an ongoing quality improvement program under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.500(a)(8) (APP-01).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the QI program, sets performance expectations, and reviews QI results at least twice a year.
Leads the QI Committee, ensures data collection, runs the problem detection and resolution system, and maintains QI records.
Reviews data, sets targets and benchmarks, adopts the QI Plan and improvement plans, and monitors results.
Supplies clinical indicator data and leads clinical improvement actions.
Report problems, take part in surveys and improvement efforts, and carry out assigned actions.

documentation: Written QI Plan (annual)
QI Committee minutes
QI Dashboard with indicators, targets and benchmarks
Resident and representative satisfaction surveys and tabulated results
Concern Log with assigned actions and closure dates
Performance improvement plans and re-measurement results
Quality improvement proof included in the license application packet (295.500(a)(8))

policies.category: Subpart B – Policies: § 295.2070 Negotiated Risk Agreement
policies.title: Negotiated Risk Agreements
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] uses a negotiated risk agreement with a resident who chooses an activity or arrangement that carries risk, so that the resident's choice is respected, the risk is understood, and a plan to reduce the risk is written and followed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] may enter into a negotiated risk agreement only with the informed agreement of the resident or the resident's representative. The agreement documents the risk, the resident's choice and the plan to reduce the risk. It is referenced in the resident's service plan and ties to the risk management statement that must appear in every establishment contract (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2030). The agreement includes all content required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2070. The Administrator checks the required content against the current text of that section before this manual is adopted and at each annual policy review, and revises the Negotiated Risk Agreement form to match. A negotiated risk agreement does not replace the admission and retention criteria in RES-01 and RES-02 and is not used to admit or keep a resident whose needs [AGENCY NAME] cannot safely meet.

definitions.definition: A written agreement between the resident (or representative) and [AGENCY NAME] that records a resident's informed choice to accept a specific risk, and the steps both parties will take to manage that risk.
The statement in the establishment contract describing how [AGENCY NAME] addresses resident choices that involve risk (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2030(a)).
Agreement given voluntarily after the resident or representative has been told the nature of the risk, likely consequences, and alternatives, in language the person understands.

procedures: A negotiated risk agreement is considered when a resident (or representative) wants to make a choice that staff believe carries a risk to the resident's health or safety, or when it is identified at assessment or reassessment (CARE-01). Staff do not start the process on their own to pressure a resident into a choice.
The nurse or care lead reviews the request with the Administrator within 3 business days and decides whether an agreement is appropriate, using RES-01, RES-02 and the resident's current assessment.

If the choice would take the resident outside the admission or retention criteria, or if the establishment lacks the staff or services to support it safely, the Administrator tells the resident and representative and does not enter into the agreement. The matter is handled under RES-01 or TERM-01.

The nurse or care lead and the Administrator meet with the resident, the representative if any, and anyone the resident wants present, such as a family member, an essential support person (ESP-01) or the physician. The meeting is held in the resident's preferred language, with interpreter or communication help as needed (RTS-06).

At the meeting, staff describe the specific risk in plain language, likely consequences, how likely they are, and the alternatives. They listen to the resident's reasons and preferences and record what the resident wants.
The group works out a mitigation plan: what the resident will do, what staff will do, any equipment or monitoring, when and how the plan will be reviewed, and who is responsible for each step.

Staff confirm the resident understands the risk and agrees voluntarily. If the resident's capacity to understand is in doubt, staff involve the resident's representative (RTS-03) and the physician as required by law, and do not rely on the resident's signature alone.

The agreement is written on the Negotiated Risk Agreement form. It records the risk, the resident's choice, the mitigation plan, the review date, the date signed, and every item required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2070. It is signed by the resident or representative and by the Administrator or designee.
The resident or representative receives a copy of the signed agreement. The original is placed in the resident's record (REC-01).

The service plan is updated within 7 days of signing to reference the agreement and the mitigation steps (CARE-01). The agreement is consistent with the risk management statement in the resident's contract (CON-01).

Staff who serve the resident are told of the agreement and their part in the mitigation plan at the next shift huddle, and a note is posted in the care instructions where appropriate. Information is shared only with those who need it (RTS-05).

The agreement is reviewed on the date set in the plan, at each reassessment, and promptly after any incident or change of condition. It may be amended or ended at any time at the resident's request, or when it no longer works. Changes are in writing and signed.

If a resident declines to agree to a mitigation plan, or the risk becomes one that [AGENCY NAME] cannot safely manage, the Administrator discusses options with the resident and representative and decides next steps under RES-01 and TERM-01, with notice given as those policies require.
The Administrator reviews all active agreements quarterly for the Quality Improvement Committee (QI-01) and records outcomes, such as incidents tied to an agreement.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether an agreement is appropriate, signs it, ensures it matches the current rule text, and reviews active agreements quarterly.
Leads the risk discussion, drafts the mitigation plan, updates the service plan, and informs direct care staff.
Makes the informed choice, takes part in the plan, and signs the agreement.
Carry out their parts of the mitigation plan and report concerns or incidents.

documentation: Signed Negotiated Risk Agreement (copy to resident or representative, original in the record)
Notes of the risk discussion, including alternatives offered
Updated service plan referencing the agreement
Review and amendment records
Quarterly active agreements report to QI Committee

policies.category: Subpart B – Policies: § 295.2080 Essential Support Persons
policies.title: Essential Support Persons and Resident Access
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident can designate an essential support person, that the designation is recorded, and that visiting and access limits never override resident rights.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] allows each resident (or the resident's representative) to designate one or more essential support persons. The designation is recorded in the resident file. [AGENCY NAME] does not restrict visiting or access in a way that overrides resident rights (RTS-01). The terms and any limits on access are those set by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2080, which the Administrator checks against the current rule text before adoption of this manual and at each annual policy review, and updates the form and procedures to match. Any limit on access that is allowed by the rule or by law is applied only to the extent allowed, for the shortest time necessary, in writing, and with notice to the resident and the essential support person.

definitions.definition: A person, such as a family member, friend or other person, whom the resident chooses to provide emotional, physical or other support and who is recognized by [AGENCY NAME] under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2080.
The resident's (or representative's) written or documented choice of an essential support person.
The ability of the essential support person to visit and be with the resident, subject only to limits permitted by the rule and by law.

procedures: At admission, and at each reassessment, staff explain to the resident and representative that the resident may designate an essential support person, and give a copy of this policy (CON-01, RTS-01).

If the resident wishes to designate someone, the resident (or representative) completes the Essential Support Person Designation Form giving the person's name, relationship, contact information, and the resident's preferences for how and when the person is involved.

Staff confirm the choice directly with the resident, privately and in the resident's language (RTS-06). If the resident cannot express a choice, staff consult the resident's representative (RTS-03) and record the basis for the designation.
The Administrator or designee records the designation in the resident file, notes it in the service plan if the person has a role in care, and informs staff who need to know (RTS-05).
A resident may change or withdraw a designation at any time. Staff record the change, with date, on the form on the same day.

The essential support person is welcomed at the establishment during the hours and under the conditions set by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2080 and [AGENCY NAME]'s visitor policy (DL-02), which may not be more restrictive than the rule or resident rights allow.

Staff do not refuse, delay or end an essential support person's access without the Administrator's approval. Before any limit is applied, the Administrator confirms that the limit is permitted by the rule and by law (for example infection control under CARE-03, a public health directive, or a safety concern about conduct) and that it is no broader or longer than necessary.

If access is limited, the Administrator tells the resident, the representative and the essential support person promptly, in writing, with the reason, the expected duration and the date of the next review. Alternatives such as outdoor visits, scheduled visits, or phone and video contact are offered where they are possible.
The Administrator reviews each limit at least weekly and ends it as soon as the reason no longer applies.

The essential support person is expected to follow reasonable safety and infection control rules, such as screening and personal protective equipment, which staff explain clearly and apply equally to all.

A resident or essential support person who believes access has been wrongly limited may use the grievance process (RTS-04), including contact with the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program. Staff give help with this on request, and no retaliation is permitted.
Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually (PER-06). The Administrator reviews designations and any limits on access quarterly for the Quality Improvement Committee (QI-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures designations are honored, approves and reviews any access limit, and keeps this policy aligned with the current rule text.
Explains the right to designate, assists with the form, and records the designation in the service plan when relevant.
Welcome essential support persons, never limit access on their own authority, and refer questions to the Administrator.
Choose and may change the essential support person.

documentation: Essential Support Person Designation Form in the resident file
Service plan notation, where applicable
Written notice and review log for any access limitation
Grievance records related to access (RTS-04)
Staff training records

policies.category: Subpart C – Personnel: § 295.3000 Personnel Requirements, Qualifications and Training
policies.title: Staffing Sufficiency, Supervision and Personnel Schedules
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] always has enough qualified, trained staff to meet the 24-hour scheduled and unscheduled needs of residents, to document who actually worked, and to keep residents who cannot move to safety by themselves protected around the clock.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains staff sufficient in number, with qualifications, adequate skills, education and experience, to meet the 24-hour scheduled and unscheduled needs of residents, and staff take part in ongoing training to serve the resident population. This policy meets 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000(a) and Section 35(a)(3) of the Act (210 ILCS 9/35). This policy meets 295.3000(h)(1)–(7): staffing covers all mandatory services, services in each service plan, general supervision and crisis intervention, food services if provided, environmental services, evacuation of residents during emergencies, and optional services stated in the service plan. This policy meets 295.3000(i)(1)–(3): the personnel schedule shows date, scheduled work hours and the name and position of each employee, reflects actual hours worked, and is kept and available on request for at least 12 months after the last date on the schedule. This policy meets 295.3000(j): if residents cannot independently move to an area of safety, enough staff are present and awake 24 hours a day to move them. [AGENCY NAME] does not accept or retain a resident when it lacks staff appropriate in number and skill to meet that resident's needs (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2000). Minimum 24-hour coverage and CPR requirements are in PER-02.

definitions.definition: Employees who provide hands-on assistance and supervision to residents, such as help with personal care, mobility, medication reminders and monitoring.
Care and services planned in advance and written in each resident's service plan.
Needs that arise without notice, such as a fall, a sudden illness, a call for help, or a behavioral or emergency situation.
The record of date, scheduled work hours, and name and position of each employee assigned, corrected to show actual hours worked.

definitions.term: Resident who cannot independently move to safety
definitions.definition: A resident whose impairment prevents the resident from reaching an area of safety without staff help, for example during a fire or other emergency.

procedures: The Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] is responsible for staffing. Before the license application is filed and before each admission, the Administrator documents that the planned staffing meets the needs of the current and incoming residents (RES-01, CARE-01).

The Administrator prepares a Staffing Plan listing, for each shift and day of the week, the number and position of staff needed to cover each of the seven areas in 295.3000(h): (1) all mandatory services (CARE-02); (2) services in each resident's service plan; (3) the resident needs, including 24-hour scheduled and unscheduled needs, general supervision and the ability to intervene in a crisis; (4) food services, if provided (FOOD-01); (5) environmental services such as housekeeping, laundry and maintenance (PP-02); (6) evacuation of residents during emergencies (PP-03, DIS-01); and (7) any optional services stated in the service plan.

The Staffing Plan is based on the actual residents' needs, using the comprehensive assessments and service plans, including residents' level of mobility, cognition, behaviors, medication needs and time of day when help is most needed. It is not based on a fixed ratio alone.

The Staffing Plan identifies required skills and qualifications for each task, including licensed or certified staff for tasks that require them (PER-04, MED-02), and confirms that each person assigned is qualified and has the required training (PER-06) before working independently.

At each pre-admission assessment, each reassessment and each change of condition, the nurse or care lead tells the Administrator whether the resident's needs change the staffing required. The Administrator documents the review in the resident's file and the Staffing Plan. This is how staffing is reviewed against resident acuity at each assessment.

If staffing is not adequate for a prospective resident, the Administrator does not admit that person. If staffing becomes inadequate for a current resident, the Administrator increases staffing right away, arranges added services, or begins the process in TERM-01 if the need cannot be met. [AGENCY NAME] does not accept or retain residents it lacks staff to serve.

The Administrator or designee prepares the personnel schedule at least 2 weeks ahead, showing the date, scheduled work hours, and name and position of every employee assigned. It includes all shifts, including nights, weekends and holidays.

The schedule shows that at least one staff member is awake, on duty and on site 24 hours a day and that at least one direct care staff person on duty at all times holds current adult CPR certification (PER-02). Shared housing schedules show at least one staff member on site at all times.

A call-off or no-show is covered immediately from the on-call/float list in writing, and the Administrator is told at once if a shift cannot be filled to the Staffing Plan level. The shift is never left below the minimum required staffing, and agency or temporary staff must meet the same qualification and background check requirements (PER-04).

The charge staff member or designee corrects the personnel schedule every shift so that it reflects the actual hours worked, including late arrivals, early departures, swaps and overtime. Corrections are initialed and dated, and the original entry is not erased.
The Administrator compares scheduled hours with time and payroll records each pay period and resolves differences, so the personnel schedule is accurate.

The Administrator identifies residents who cannot independently move to an area of safety, as recorded in the assessment, service plan and evacuation roster. For these residents, enough staff are present and awake 24 hours a day to move them to a safe area, based on the number of such residents, their needs and how the building is laid out (295.3000(j)). The Administrator tests this at drills and records the results (DIS-03).
The Administrator provides general supervision of staff through regular rounds on all shifts and makes sure a manager or supervisor can be reached at all times at [PHONE] for crisis intervention.

Staffing is reviewed at least monthly and any time there is a serious incident, resident complaint, survey finding or staff shortage. Findings and actions go to the Quality Improvement Committee quarterly (QI-01).
Staff are given continuing training that fits the resident population, such as dementia care, fall prevention, infection control and emergency procedures (PER-06, CARE-04).

Personnel schedules, with actual hours worked, are retained and available on request for at least 12 months after the last date on the schedule and are not purged earlier. The Administrator makes them available to IDPH surveyors on request. Failure to maintain required staffing or admitting residents beyond the establishment's capacity to serve can result in citations and civil penalties under the Act (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Sets and reviews the Staffing Plan, approves schedules, decides on admissions and retention based on staffing, and ensures records are kept.
Reports changes in resident needs that affect staffing and helps with the skill mix needed.
Confirms that every shift meets minimum staffing, covers call-offs, and records actual hours worked.
Report as scheduled, complete required training, and tell the supervisor if staffing seems inadequate.
Provides the budget and resources needed to meet staffing requirements.

documentation: Written Staffing Plan covering the seven areas in 295.3000(h)
Personnel schedules (date, scheduled hours, name and position) corrected to actual hours worked
Records of staffing review at each assessment and change of condition
Roster of residents who cannot move independently to safety and awake-staff coverage record
Call-off and coverage log
Time/payroll comparison records
Training records (PER-06)

policies.category: Subpart C – Personnel: § 295.3000 Personnel Requirements, Qualifications and Training
policies.title: 24-Hour On-Site Coverage and CPR-Certified Direct Care Staff
policies.applies_to: All employees and scheduling staff of [AGENCY NAME]; assisted living and shared housing establishments (the rule differs by type, as set out below)
policies.purpose: To make sure a qualified staff member is on site every hour of every day, and that at least one direct care staff person on every shift can give adult CPR, so residents' scheduled and unscheduled needs are met at all times.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] staffs each shift so that on-site coverage and CPR coverage are never interrupted. This policy meets 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000(b), 295.3000(k) and 295.3000(l).

295.3000(b) – CPR-certified direct care staff: At least one direct care staff person with current adult CPR certification, including a demonstration of ability (a hands-on skills check), is on duty at all times. An online-only course without a skills demonstration does not count toward this requirement.

295.3000(l) – Assisted living: [AGENCY NAME] has at least one staff member awake, on duty and on site 24 hours per day. That person must be awake for the whole shift.

295.3000(k) – Shared housing: [AGENCY NAME] has at least one staff member on site at all times. The only exception is a brief absence, such as an emergency room trip or a grocery trip. During a brief absence, arrangements are made to monitor resident safety in accordance with each affected resident's service delivery plan.

This policy supports the Act's requirement that staffing be sufficient in number and skill to meet residents' 24-hour scheduled and unscheduled needs (210 ILCS 9/35(a)(3); 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000(a)). See PER-01 for overall staffing sufficiency. [AGENCY NAME] operates as a [assisted living establishment / shared housing establishment]; only the rule for that license type applies to the schedule, but the CPR rule applies to both.

definitions.definition: Employees who provide hands-on care or services to residents, such as personal care, medication assistance or supervision.

definitions.term: Awake, on duty and on site
definitions.definition: The staff member is physically in the establishment, is performing duties, and is not sleeping at any time during the shift. This is the assisted living standard.

definitions.term: Current adult CPR certification with demonstration of ability
definitions.definition: An unexpired adult CPR card from a recognized training provider, earned after an in-person or live skills check on a manikin.
A short, unavoidable absence of the only on-site staff member, such as an emergency room trip or a grocery trip, during which resident safety is monitored under the service delivery plan.

procedures: The Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], builds the weekly staff schedule at least [14] days ahead. It must show a named on-site staff member for every hour of the 24-hour day, including nights, weekends and holidays.

For each shift on the schedule, the scheduler marks which direct care staff person holds current adult CPR certification. A shift without a CPR-certified direct care staff person may not be published or worked.

Assisted living only: the schedule names the staff member who is awake, on duty and on site for every overnight shift. That person stays awake and does not sleep, whether in a resident area or elsewhere.
Shared housing only: the schedule names the staff member who is on site on each shift. That person does not leave except for a brief absence under steps 5 and 6.

Shared housing only: before leaving for a brief absence, the staff member tells the Administrator or on-call manager. The staff member notes the time and reason on the shift log, and does not leave if any resident's service delivery plan requires continuous on-site staff.

Shared housing only: during a brief absence, the staff member follows the monitoring arrangement in the residents' service delivery plans. Examples are a call-in check by a designated back-up person or a neighbor or other staff member within reach. The staff member logs the departure and return times.

New direct care hires must show a CPR card with a skills demonstration at hire. If they have none, the Administrator enrolls them in a skills-based course. Until certified, they are not counted as the CPR-certified person for any shift.

The Administrator keeps a CPR tracking log listing each direct care employee, the course provider, the date of the skills demonstration and the card expiration date. The log is updated whenever a card is issued or renewed.
The Administrator reviews the CPR log monthly. Any employee whose card expires within 60 days is scheduled for renewal training, and the date is entered on the log.
An employee whose CPR certification lapses is not counted toward CPR coverage until recertified. The Administrator re-checks the schedule that day to confirm every shift still has a certified person.

If a scheduled employee calls off, the shift supervisor immediately calls the [ON-CALL STAFF LIST] in order until a replacement with the needed qualification (on-site, awake if assisted living, CPR-certified if no other certified person is on the shift) is confirmed. The supervisor documents each call made.

If coverage cannot be filled, the shift supervisor contacts the Administrator at [PHONE]. The Administrator or a qualified designee reports to the building until coverage is secured. The building is never left without an on-site staff member.
A departing shift does not leave until the relieving staff member has arrived and received report. Staff do not leave a shift early if doing so would leave the building uncovered.
Each shift's actual staff, hours worked and the name of the CPR-certified employee on duty are recorded on the daily staffing record, which is signed by the shift supervisor.

The Administrator checks the daily staffing records weekly against the posted schedule, investigates any gap and records corrective action. Coverage gaps are reported to the Governing Body and reviewed in the quality improvement program (QI-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures 24-hour on-site coverage and CPR coverage on every shift; maintains the CPR tracking log; arranges coverage when call-offs occur.
Builds schedules that meet the rule, finds replacements, completes daily staffing records and logs brief absences.
Stay on site (and awake, in assisted living) throughout the shift, keep CPR certification current, and report any lapse or coverage problem at once.
Provides the staff and funding needed to maintain continuous coverage and reviews coverage gaps.

documentation: Posted weekly staff schedules showing on-site staff and CPR-certified staff for every shift
CPR tracking log with card copies, skills-demonstration evidence and expiration dates
Daily staffing records signed by the shift supervisor
Shift log entries for brief absences in shared housing (time out, time in, reason, monitoring arrangement)
Call-off and replacement call records
Quality improvement notes on coverage gaps and corrective action

policies.category: Subpart C – Personnel: § 295.3000 Personnel Requirements, Qualifications and Training
policies.title: Job Descriptions, Minimum Age, Employee Files and Personnel Record Retention
policies.applies_to: Administrator, human resources designee and all hiring staff of [AGENCY NAME]; all employees and persons providing service under contract
policies.purpose: To make sure every position has a written job description with minimum education and experience, direct care staff meet the minimum age, and a complete, protected file is kept for every employee for the required period.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] hires only people who meet the written qualifications for their positions and keeps a complete personnel file for every employee. This policy meets 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000(c), (d), (e), (f) and (g).

295.3000(c) – Minimum age: At the starting date of employment, each direct care staff member is 16 years of age or older.

295.3000(d) – Job descriptions: Written job descriptions define the minimum education and experience requirements for each staff position.

295.3000(e) – Employee files: A file is kept for each employee containing (1) name, date of birth, home address, Social Security number and telephone number; (2) documentation of (A) freedom from pulmonary tuberculosis, (B) employee orientation and (C) ongoing training; and (3) starting and ending dates of employment.

295.3000(f) – Direct care employee files: The file for each direct care employee also contains documentation of (1) current CPR certification, if applicable; (2) initial health evaluation; (3) compliance with the Health Care Worker Background Check Act (225 ILCS 46); and (4) that the employer checked the employee's status with the Nurse Aide Registry.

295.3000(g) – Retention: Records required by this Section are maintained throughout employment or service and for at least 12 months after the last date of employment or service, unless State or federal law requires a longer period. [AGENCY NAME] applies the longer period whenever another law or its payer requires one.

definitions.definition: An employee who provides hands-on care or services to residents. These employees need the additional file items in 295.3000(f).
The confidential record, in paper or secure electronic form, holding the items required by 295.3000(e) and (f) and other employment documents.
The first day the person works for [AGENCY NAME] in any capacity. The age rule is measured on this date.

procedures: The Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], writes and approves a job description for every position, including Administrator/Manager, direct care staff, medication aide (if used), dietary, housekeeping and maintenance. Each description states the minimum education and experience required.

Job descriptions are signed and dated by the Administrator and reviewed at least annually and whenever duties change. Employees receive a copy of their job description at hire and sign an acknowledgment.

Before an offer is made, the hiring staff member compares the applicant's education and experience to the job description. The comparison is documented on the hiring checklist. An applicant who does not meet the minimums is not hired into that position.

For direct care positions, the hiring staff member verifies date of birth from a government-issued ID. An applicant who is not 16 on the starting date is not hired as direct care staff. A copy of the ID is placed in the file.

On or before the first day of work, the human resources designee opens a personnel file and records the employee's name, date of birth, home address, Social Security number and telephone number (295.3000(e)(1)).
The designee records the starting date of employment in the file. When employment ends, the designee records the ending date within 5 working days (295.3000(e)(3)).

The employee file receives documentation of freedom from pulmonary tuberculosis (see PER-07), documentation of orientation (see PER-06) and a training record that is added to as ongoing training is completed (295.3000(e)(2)).

For direct care employees, the file also holds: a copy of the current CPR card with skills demonstration, if the employee holds one (295.3000(f)(1)); the initial health evaluation (295.3000(f)(2)); documentation of compliance with the Health Care Worker Background Check Act (295.3000(f)(3)); and the dated Nurse Aide Registry check result (295.3000(f)(4)). See PER-04.

The human resources designee audits each new file with the Personnel File Checklist within 30 days of hire and again at each annual review. Missing items are listed with a due date. The Administrator initials the checklist when the file is complete.
The Administrator performs a quarterly spot audit of at least [5] files or all files if fewer. Findings and corrections are recorded and reported in the quality improvement program (QI-01).
