The business office stops service charges according to the contract. Within the time stated in the contract refund policy, it calculates any refund of fees and deposits and prepares a final accounting.
Resident funds held by [AGENCY NAME] and personal property are inventoried and released to the representative or estate representative, with signatures, under CON-03.
The Administrator closes the record and retains it under REC-01. The Administrator offers support to staff and other residents after a death and records any follow-up needed.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether the hospice arrangement can be supported, ensures the service plan is revised, directs notifications after a death, and ensures refund and funds settlement.
Coordinates daily with hospice or home health, updates the service plan and advises direct care staff.
Provide the care in the service plan, report changes, and follow procedures at the time of death.
Calculates the final account and refunds under the contract and arranges release of funds.
Provides its licensed services under its plan of care and shares updates with [AGENCY NAME].

documentation: Verification of hospice or home health license and contact information
Signed agreement of all parties to the hospice arrangement
Hospice plan of care and the revised service plan
Communication log with the hospice
Notification log following a death, with date, time, person and method
IDPH report (if required) under INC-01
Final account, refund calculation and receipt for funds and property released
Closed record retained under REC-01

policies.category: Subpart E – Medications (§ 295.5000)
policies.title: Medication Reminders, Self-Administration Supervision, Administration, Storage and Disposal
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment – Administrator, licensed nurses, certified medication aides and direct care staff
policies.purpose: To state which medication services [AGENCY NAME] offers, who may provide each service, and how medications are stored, handled, recorded and disposed of safely.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides medication services at the three levels defined in 210 ILCS 9/70: medication reminders, supervision of self-administered medication, and medication administration. Medication administration is performed only by a licensed health care professional employed by [AGENCY NAME], or by a certified medication aide acting under RN supervision and delegation (see MED-02). Supervision of self-administered medication is performed under a licensed health care professional, or under RN delegation for a certified medication aide. The services offered to each resident are stated in the establishment contract and the service plan. Storage, record keeping and procedures meet IDPH's medication rules in Subpart E. Public Act 104-0589 amended Section 70, so the Administrator reviews the current text of the Act and the rule at every annual policy review (GOV-01).

definitions.definition: A service within the meaning of 210 ILCS 9/70 in which staff remind a resident that it is time to take a medication the resident takes without hands-on help. Staff do not open containers, handle or dispense medication.

A service within the meaning of 210 ILCS 9/70 in which a qualified person oversees a resident who takes his or her own medication. It is provided under a licensed health care professional, or under RN delegation for a certified medication aide.

A service within the meaning of 210 ILCS 9/70 in which a qualified person gives a medication to the resident, or assists directly in giving it. Only a licensed health care professional employed by [AGENCY NAME], or a delegated certified medication aide, may do this.
An individual licensed in Illinois whose license permits the task, and who is employed by [AGENCY NAME].
A certified individual who may administer medication under RN supervision and delegation as described in MED-02.

procedures: During pre-admission assessment (CARE-01), the nurse records all prescription and non-prescription medications, supplements and treatments, with the prescriber and dose, and notes the resident's ability to manage them.

The Administrator and nurse decide which service level the resident needs: reminders, supervision of self-administration, or administration. The decision is explained to the resident and representative and written into the service plan and the contract (CON-01).
Staff provide only the service level in the service plan. If a resident's ability changes, staff tell the nurse the same day and the service plan is updated under CARE-01 and CARE-05.

Medication reminders: staff give a verbal reminder at the scheduled time and note on the Medication Reminder Record whether the resident took the medication, refused it, or was not available. Staff do not handle the medication.

Supervision of self-administered medication: only a licensed health care professional, or a certified medication aide under RN delegation, supervises. The supervisor observes the resident, redirects errors and records each dose on the Medication Record.

Administration: only a licensed health care professional employed by [AGENCY NAME], or a certified medication aide under RN delegation (MED-02), may administer. The person verifies the right resident, medication, dose, route and time against the prescriber's order before each dose.
Before assigning anyone to administer or supervise, the Administrator verifies license or certification under PER-04 and records the verification in the employee file.
Each dose given, refused, held or missed is recorded on the Medication Record at the time of the event, with the initials or signature of the person who provided the service.

Medications are stored in their original labeled containers in a locked cabinet or locked drawer in the resident's unit or in a locked medication area. Only authorized staff hold keys. Medications requiring refrigeration are kept in a locked container or refrigerator at the temperature on the label, and the temperature is logged daily.

Medications for external use are stored apart from oral medications. Residents who self-store medications in their units are assessed for safety, and a lockable storage place is provided when the assessment shows a risk to other residents.

Medication errors, refusals with clinical impact, and adverse reactions are reported to the nurse immediately. The nurse notifies the prescriber and representative and records the event on a Medication Variance Report the same day. Errors resulting in harm are reviewed for reporting under INC-01.
Controlled medications are counted at each shift change by two staff members with a signed count sheet. Any discrepancy is reported to the Administrator immediately and investigated.

Discontinued, expired or contaminated medications and those belonging to a deceased or discharged resident are removed from the resident's supply. They are disposed of in the manner required by IDPH rules and law, by two staff members who record the medication, amount, date, method and signatures on the Medication Disposal Record. Medications are returned to the resident or representative upon discharge when permitted.
The nurse reviews medication records at least monthly for completeness, accuracy and variances, and reports trends to the Quality Improvement Program (QI-01).
The Administrator reviews this policy against the current text of 210 ILCS 9/70, as amended by Public Act 104-0589, and the current IDPH rule at the annual policy review, and records the review date.

responsibilities.duty: Decides which medication services are offered, verifies licenses and certifications, and reviews this policy against current law.

responsibilities.role: Licensed nurse (RN or other licensed professional employed by [AGENCY NAME])
responsibilities.duty: Assesses medication needs, administers medications, supervises and delegates as the law allows, reviews records and responds to errors.
Administers or supervises only within the RN's written delegation, and records each dose.

responsibilities.role: Direct care staff (not licensed or certified)
responsibilities.duty: Give medication reminders only and report any concern to the nurse. They do not handle, supervise or administer medication.
Provide accurate medication information, agree to the service level, and report problems.

documentation: Medication list and assessment of the resident's ability to manage medications
Service plan and contract entries showing the medication service level
Medication Reminder Record and Medication Record
Controlled medication count sheets
Refrigerator temperature log
Medication Variance Reports
Medication Disposal Record
License and certification verification
Annual policy review note

policies.category: Subpart E – Medications (§ 295.5000)
policies.title: Certified Medication Aides and RN Delegation
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment – Administrator, supervising RN and certified medication aides
policies.purpose: To make sure any certified medication aide working at [AGENCY NAME] is qualified, properly supervised by an RN, and limited to tasks the law allows.
policies.policy: A certified medication aide may administer medication at [AGENCY NAME] only under the supervision and delegation of an RN, as provided by the Nurse Practice Act (Sections 50-75) and 210 ILCS 9/70. A certified medication aide may not administer Schedule II controlled substances, or any subcutaneous, intramuscular, intradermal or IV medication. Supervision of self-administered medication may be done by a certified medication aide only under RN delegation. The Administrator verifies each license and certification before duties are assigned and keeps the records in the employee file.

definitions.definition: A staff member who holds the Illinois certification that permits medication administration under RN supervision and delegation.
A written decision by a registered nurse to assign a specific medication task to a specific, qualified individual and to supervise that individual under the Nurse Practice Act.
Schedule II controlled substances and any subcutaneous, intramuscular, intradermal or IV medication, which a certified medication aide may not administer.

procedures: Before a staff member is assigned medication duties, the Administrator verifies the individual's medication aide certification and any related license, and checks the Nurse Aide Registry as required by PER-04. The date, source and result of verification are recorded in the employee file.

The Administrator rechecks the status of each certification before its expiration date and at least annually. A person with an expired, suspended or revoked certification is removed from medication duties the same day.
The supervising RN, who is employed or engaged by [AGENCY NAME], reviews the certified medication aide's competence and training before delegating any task.

The RN writes each delegation, identifying the aide, the residents or tasks covered, the allowed medication categories and limitations, and the date. The delegation is signed by the RN and the aide and kept in the employee file.

The RN states in each delegation that Schedule II controlled substances and all subcutaneous, intramuscular, intradermal and IV medications are excluded. The aide may not give them even in an emergency.
The aide may supervise a resident's self-administered medication only when the RN has delegated that task for that resident, and the service plan shows that level of service (MED-01).
The RN is available by phone to the aide during every shift in which the aide does medication duties. The on-call number is posted in the medication area as [PHONE].
The RN evaluates the aide's work through direct observation and record review at least [FREQUENCY – e.g., monthly] and after any medication error. Findings are documented in the employee file.
The aide reports refusals, errors, adverse reactions and changes in condition to the RN immediately. The RN notifies the prescriber and representative as in MED-01 and CARE-05.
The aide records each dose on the Medication Record immediately after the task. The RN reviews the records for accuracy during the monthly review in MED-01.

If a medication order includes a Schedule II drug or an injected or IV medication, a licensed health care professional employed by [AGENCY NAME] provides it, or [AGENCY NAME] arranges an outside licensed provider with the resident's consent as permitted by 210 ILCS 9/70.
The RN may withdraw or change a delegation at any time for a clinical or safety reason. The Administrator removes the aide from the affected duties the same day and records the change.
The Administrator reviews the roster of certified medication aides at least quarterly and reports medication-related events to the Quality Improvement Program (QI-01).

responsibilities.duty: Verifies licenses and certifications before assigning duties, rechecks them, and removes any staff member whose status lapses.
Delegates in writing, supervises and evaluates the aide, stays reachable, and withdraws delegation when needed.
Works only within the written delegation and the legal limits, records each dose, and reports concerns.
Includes delegation compliance and medication events in QI reviews.

documentation: Certification and license verification records and recheck dates
Nurse Aide Registry check (PER-04)
Signed RN delegations and any withdrawals
RN supervision and competency evaluations
Medication Records completed by the aide
Medication Variance Reports
On-call RN contact list
Quarterly roster review

policies.category: Subpart F – Resident Rights (§ 295.6000–295.6030)
policies.title: Resident Rights and Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment – all staff, residents and representatives
policies.purpose: To protect the rights of every resident, to make sure residents and representatives know those rights, and to make sure staff honor them.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects and protects the rights of residents listed in Section 95 of the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act and IDPH's resident rights rule. The establishment contract lists the Section 95 rights and states that signing the contract does not forfeit any of them (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2030). Rights are given to each resident or representative at admission, posted in a visible place, acknowledged in writing, and taught to every staff member at orientation. [AGENCY NAME] complies with the Americans with Disabilities Act by making reasonable modifications and providing accessible communication and facilities. Residents also have responsibilities, which are explained at admission and are not used to deny any right.

definitions.definition: The list of resident rights in Section 95 of the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act that must be printed in the establishment contract. The current full text is kept in the Resident Rights binder.
A person legally authorized or designated by the resident to act on the resident's behalf, as described in RTS-03.
A change to a rule, practice or physical feature that lets a resident with a disability use and enjoy the establishment equally, consistent with the ADA.

procedures: The Administrator keeps the current complete text of Section 95 and IDPH's resident rights rule in the Resident Rights binder. The Administrator checks the text against the current law at each annual policy review (GOV-01).

Before the contract is signed, the Administrator or designee gives the resident and representative a copy of the rights, explains them in plain language, and answers questions. Interpreters or other aids are provided as needed (RTS-06).

The resident or representative signs a Resident Rights Acknowledgment form, which is placed in the resident record. The contract's rights list and statement that signing does not forfeit rights are reviewed with the resident (CON-01).

The rights list is posted at [LOCATION] in large print, with the Department on Aging Senior Helpline and Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program contact information, which appears in the contract and in RTS-04.

Every new employee is trained on resident rights at orientation before working alone with residents, and trained again at least annually. Attendance and a test of understanding are recorded in the employee file (PER-06).

Staff honor resident rights in daily care. Staff knock before entering a unit, offer choices, protect privacy and confidentiality (RTS-05), and do not impose restrictions that are not agreed in writing.

Any staff member who sees or learns of a possible violation of a resident right reports it to the Administrator immediately. If the concern involves abuse, neglect or exploitation, RTS-02 is followed.
Residents may raise concerns or file grievances without fear of retaliation, as stated in RTS-04. Retaliation by any staff member is grounds for discipline up to termination.

For residents with disabilities, the Administrator reviews requests for reasonable modifications within five business days. Each request, decision and reason is documented. A denial is considered only if the change would impose an undue burden or fundamentally alter the service, and the Administrator offers an alternative.

Residents' responsibilities are explained at admission: pay fees under the contract, follow the contract and posted house rules that do not violate rights, respect other residents and staff, and keep [AGENCY NAME] informed of changes in health, representative and contact details.

Where a resident's cognitive capacity limits the exercise of a right, the representative acts under RTS-03 and the resident still takes part in decisions as far as possible. Rights restricted by safety needs are addressed only through a negotiated risk process (NRA-01) or other lawful written process.
The Administrator reviews complaints and any alleged rights violations monthly and reports patterns to the Quality Improvement Program (QI-01).
A copy of the rights is given again whenever the contract is renewed or amended, and on request at any time.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains current rights text, gives and explains rights at admission, ensures staff training, reviews modification requests and investigates alleged violations.
Know and honor the rights, report possible violations, and never retaliate.
Learn the rights, sign the acknowledgment, and meet the responsibilities stated at admission.
Provides and records resident rights training.

documentation: Resident Rights binder with current Section 95 text
Signed Resident Rights Acknowledgment in each record
Establishment contract showing rights list (CON-01)
Photograph or log of the posted rights notice
Orientation and annual training records
Reasonable modification request log and decisions
Grievance and complaint log (RTS-04)

policies.category: Subpart F – Resident Rights (§ 295.6000–295.6030)
policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Financial Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment – all employees, volunteers, contractors, residents and representatives
policies.purpose: To prevent abuse, neglect and financial exploitation of residents, to make sure suspected incidents are reported promptly and investigated, and to protect residents and reporters from harm and retaliation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, misappropriation of resident property and financial exploitation. We screen every employee with resident contact through the Nurse Aide Registry check before hire (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000) and the Health Care Worker Background Check Act (225 ILCS 46), with fingerprints collected electronically and sent to the Illinois State Police within 10 working days. [AGENCY NAME] does not hire anyone with a Registry finding of abuse, neglect or misappropriation of property. All staff must report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately. Serious harm is reported to IDPH within 24 hours at DPH.LTCAL@illinois.gov. The agencies, time frames and training content required by IDPH's rule on abuse and neglect are followed and are reviewed at every annual policy review. Retaliation against any resident, family member or staff reporter is prohibited. [AGENCY NAME] understands that IDPH may assess civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation, with each day a separate violation (210 ILCS 9/135).

definitions.definition: Any physical, sexual, verbal or emotional mistreatment of a resident, including intimidation, humiliation, unreasonable confinement and inappropriate restraint.
Failure to provide the care, supervision, food, medication or services a resident needs to avoid harm, whether or not intentional.
Improper use, taking, withholding or control of a resident's money, property or benefits, including by coercion, deception or undue influence.
Abuse, neglect or exploitation that results in injury, serious change in condition, death or a significant risk of any of these. It is reported to IDPH within 24 hours.
Any adverse action against a resident, family member or employee for reporting or cooperating in a report or investigation.

procedures: Prevention – hiring: Before an employee has resident contact, the Administrator checks the Nurse Aide Registry and does not hire anyone with a finding of abuse, neglect or misappropriation of resident property (295.3000). The check date and result are recorded in the employee file (PER-04).

Prevention – background checks: The Administrator collects fingerprints electronically for each applicant who has or may have resident contact and transmits them to the Illinois State Police within 10 working days, as required by the Health Care Worker Background Check Act (225 ILCS 46). Results are filed and acted on as the Act requires.

Prevention – training: Every employee receives training at orientation, before working alone, and at least annually on recognizing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation, resident rights, dementia behaviors and de-escalation (PER-06). Training follows the content IDPH's rule requires.

Prevention – supervision: The Administrator keeps staffing sufficient under PER-01, reviews high-risk times and locations, and encourages residents to share concerns. Staff do not handle a resident's money or property except as CON-03 permits.

Prevention – finances: Staff may not borrow from, accept gifts above a nominal value from, or become a beneficiary or agent of a resident. Any resident funds held follow the accounting and receipt requirements in CON-03.

Reporting by staff: Any employee who sees, suspects or is told of abuse, neglect or exploitation protects the resident from immediate danger, then reports to the Administrator or, if the Administrator is involved or unavailable, to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME'S BACKUP] right away, and within the same shift. Anyone may also report directly to IDPH or other agencies.

Emergency action: Staff call 911 for any resident in danger or needing medical care or if a crime may have occurred. The alleged perpetrator is separated from the resident and does not have resident contact until the Administrator decides otherwise.

Administrator reports: The Administrator reports serious harm to IDPH within 24 hours of learning of it, by email to DPH.LTCAL@illinois.gov, and records the date, time, content and method. The Administrator also makes any other report required by the Act, IDPH rules and other Illinois law, including to law enforcement and to the representative, and keeps the current agency contact list at [LOCATION] with [PHONE].

Protection of the resident: The Administrator ensures the resident is medically evaluated, offered emotional support and, as needed, moved or given added supervision. The representative is notified the same day.

Investigation: The Administrator begins an investigation immediately and completes a written report within [NUMBER] working days, or sooner if IDPH or law enforcement requires. The report includes interviews, evidence, findings and corrective action. Staff cooperate fully with IDPH and law enforcement.

Employee action: An employee accused of abuse, neglect or exploitation is removed from resident contact during the investigation. A substantiated finding results in discipline up to termination and any report required by law, including to licensing bodies and the Nurse Aide Registry.

No retaliation: The Administrator informs all staff and residents that retaliation is prohibited. Any adverse action against a reporter within [NUMBER] days of a report is reviewed by the Administrator and the governing body.

Resident and family awareness: At admission, residents and representatives receive information about how to report concerns to the Administrator, IDPH, the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program and the Department on Aging Senior Helpline (RTS-04).
Follow-up: The Administrator tracks every report to closure, reviews trends monthly with the Quality Improvement Program (QI-01), and corrects any system failure that contributed.
Governance: The Administrator briefs the governing body quarterly on reports and outcomes and on the exposure to civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation per day (210 ILCS 9/135).

responsibilities.duty: Screens employees, ensures training, reports serious harm to IDPH within 24 hours, leads investigations, and prevents retaliation.
Report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately, protect residents, and cooperate in investigations.
Completes Registry checks and electronic fingerprint submission within 10 working days and files results.
Reviews reports, supports corrective action and provides resources.
May report concerns to any staff member, the Administrator, IDPH or the Ombudsman at any time.

Health Care Worker Background Check fingerprint submission dates and results
Orientation and annual abuse, neglect and exploitation training records
Staff reports and the Administrator's incident report
Copy and date of the 24-hour IDPH report and any other agency report
Investigation report, findings, corrective actions and discipline records
Monthly trend reports to QI-01 and governing body briefings
Posted and distributed reporting contact information

policies.category: Subpart F – Resident Rights (§ 295.6000–295.6030)
policies.title: Resident's Representative and Advance Directives
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; all residents, applicants, their representatives, and all staff who admit residents or maintain resident records
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident can be represented by a person of the resident's choosing when the resident wants or needs that help. To make sure a representative is identified, documented and used correctly. To make sure the resident's advance directives are known, kept in the record, reflected in the service plan and honored.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] recognizes a resident's right to have a representative and to make decisions for himself or herself for as long as he or she is able. A representative may take part in the service plan and may sign the establishment contract for the resident, as allowed by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2030 (C8). The agency does not appoint a representative for a resident and does not accept an applicant who cannot communicate needs unless the requirements of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2000(c)(2) (C13) are met. As the agency applies that rule, a resident who cannot communicate needs must have an appointed representative who lives in the establishment and had a prior relationship with the resident. The administrator confirms this against the current text of the rule at each annual policy review. The agency may not accept or keep a resident when it lacks staff appropriate in number and skill or cannot provide or secure the required services (C13). The agency also does not require, or pressure a resident to execute, any advance directive, and it does not make admission conditional on having one. Advance directives are kept in the resident record, noted in the service plan, and shared with emergency and hospital personnel when the resident is transferred. The agency follows the representative rules in the resident rights subpart of the Department's rules (not reproduced in this manual). Where this policy and those rules differ, the rules control.

definitions.definition: A person the resident has chosen or who is legally authorized (for example, under a power of attorney or guardianship order) to act for the resident in matters such as the contract, service plan and notices.
A written instruction recognized under Illinois law about future health care, such as a living will, a health care power of attorney, a POLST form, or a mental health declaration.
A resident who is unable, by any means, to make his or her needs and wishes known to staff.

procedures: 1. At the pre-admission inquiry, the Administrator or designee asks the applicant whether he or she wants a representative, and whether any person already holds a power of attorney, guardianship or similar authority. The answer is recorded on the admission checklist.

2. The Administrator requests a copy of any document that gives a person legal authority (power of attorney, guardianship order, health care surrogate designation) and places it in the resident record. Staff do not accept verbal claims of authority.
3. Staff give the applicant and representative a written explanation of the representative's role, including which documents the representative may sign and receive.

4. If the applicant has capacity and does not want a representative, staff note that choice in the record. The resident signs his or her own contract and service plan. The resident may name a representative later.

5. Before accepting an applicant who appears unable to communicate needs, the Administrator reviews the facts with the person who conducted the comprehensive assessment. The Administrator confirms that the 295.2000(c)(2) requirement for an appointed representative who lives in the establishment and had a prior relationship is met. The Administrator documents the finding. If the requirement is not met, the agency does not admit the applicant and gives the applicant or family a written explanation and referral suggestions.

6. The representative may sign the establishment contract for the resident, as C8 allows. The signature block shows the signer's name and the capacity in which he or she signs, and a copy of the authority document is attached. A copy of the signed contract goes to the resident or representative. The original stays on the premises.
7. At admission, the Resident Services Coordinator asks every resident (or the representative) whether the resident has advance directives. The answer is recorded.
8. If the resident has advance directives, staff obtain a copy for the record and note the directive and its location on the service plan. Staff do not interpret or change the directive.

9. If the resident has none, staff offer general information, tell the resident he or she may complete one with his or her own advisor or physician, and record that information was offered. The resident's choice not to have a directive does not affect admission or services.
10. Staff place a visible marker in the record, according to agency practice, showing that an advance directive exists and where to find it. Staff on every shift know how to locate it quickly.

11. When a resident is sent to a hospital or emergency service, the transferring staff member sends a copy of the advance directive and POLST (if any) with the transfer packet, together with the representative's contact information. (See CARE-05.)

12. If a resident's capacity changes, the Resident Services Coordinator notifies the physician and the representative and requests an updated assessment as set out in CARE-01. The service plan is revised and any needed documents on file are updated.

13. Staff direct questions about a representative's authority, or a disagreement between a representative and the resident, to the Administrator. The Administrator may ask for the legal document again and may seek legal advice. Until the question is settled, staff follow the resident's own expressed wishes wherever the resident is able to express them.

14. The Administrator reviews each resident's representative and advance directive documents at the annual reassessment and service plan review, and whenever there is a significant change in condition. Updates are recorded in the same entry as the review.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces this policy; verifies authority documents; makes the 295.2000(c)(2) determination; resolves questions about a representative's authority.
Asks about representatives and advance directives at admission and at each review; files documents; updates the service plan.
Know where advance directives are kept, never withhold them from emergency responders, and report any resident or family question to the Resident Services Coordinator.
Provide current authority documents and advance directives and tell the agency of any change.

documentation: Admission checklist entry showing the representative and advance directive questions asked
Copy of authority document (power of attorney, guardianship order or other)
Copy of advance directive, POLST or similar form
Signed contract showing the signer's capacity
Administrator's written finding for any applicant unable to communicate needs
Service plan entry noting the existence and location of advance directives
Record of annual and change-of-condition reviews of these documents

policies.category: Subpart F – Resident Rights (§ 295.6000–295.6030)
policies.title: Grievances, Complaints and Ombudsman Access
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; all residents, representatives, families, staff and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program
policies.purpose: To give residents and their representatives a clear, safe way to raise complaints, to make sure each one is heard and resolved, and to guarantee access to the Department on Aging Senior Helpline and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] welcomes complaints and treats them as a source of information for improving care. Every resident and representative may complain, orally or in writing, to any staff member or to an outside agency, without fear of retaliation. The establishment contract describes the complaint process and gives notice of the Department on Aging Senior Helpline and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program, as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2030 (C8). The agency gives the Long-Term Care Ombudsman access to residents. Every grievance and its resolution are logged and fed into the Quality Improvement program (QI-01). The agency does not retaliate against, threaten, discharge, or change the services of any resident or representative because of a complaint, and any staff member who does so is subject to discipline up to termination.

definitions.definition: Any complaint, concern or expression of dissatisfaction about care, services, staff, other residents, the environment or the agency's policies, whether made orally or in writing.
The program that advocates for residents of long-term care settings, receives and investigates complaints, and is notified to residents in the contract.
The Illinois Department on Aging helpline named in the establishment contract as a place residents may call about complaints.
Any adverse action, threat, harassment or change in treatment because a person made or supported a complaint.

procedures: 1. At admission, the Administrator or designee reviews the complaint process section of the contract with the resident and representative and gives them a written summary. The summary names the Administrator as the grievance officer and gives the Senior Helpline and Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program contact information.
2. The agency posts, where residents and visitors can see it, the grievance process, the Administrator's name and the current numbers: [SENIOR HELPLINE PHONE] and [REGIONAL OMBUDSMAN PHONE].

3. Any staff member who receives a complaint listens, writes down the details on the Grievance Form the same day, and gives it to the Administrator by the end of the shift. Staff may not refuse, discourage or delay a complaint. A resident may also complain without staff help.
4. The Administrator enters the grievance in the Grievance Log the next business day. The entry shows the date, the complainant, the issue, and who is assigned to look into it.
5. The Administrator acknowledges the grievance to the complainant, orally or in writing, within 2 business days. This is the agency's own standard.

6. If the complaint alleges abuse, neglect, financial exploitation or a serious injury, the Administrator immediately follows RTS-02 and INC-01 in place of the ordinary grievance steps. The grievance log notes the cross-reference.
7. The Administrator, or a person designated who is not the subject of the complaint, looks into the issue, speaks with the resident and any involved staff, and reviews the records.

8. The Administrator gives the complainant a written response within 10 business days (the agency's standard). The response states what was found, what action was taken, and the resident's right to contact the Senior Helpline, the Ombudsman, or IDPH if dissatisfied. If more time is needed, the Administrator explains why and gives a new date.

9. The Administrator records the resolution and the complainant's satisfaction (satisfied, partly satisfied or not satisfied) in the log. If the resident is not satisfied, the Administrator offers to meet with the resident and representative and offers contact information for the Ombudsman.
10. The Administrator keeps the identity of a complainant confidential and tells only the people who need to know in order to resolve the matter.

11. Ombudsman access: when a representative of the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program arrives, staff admit him or her at once, ask the Ombudsman to show identification, and notify the Administrator. Staff provide a private place to talk with any resident who wishes to talk. Staff do not listen in, and they provide records only as the resident or the law permits.
12. If an Ombudsman complaint is made about the establishment, the Administrator cooperates fully, supplies requested information as the law permits, and logs the contact and the outcome.

13. Staff may never tell a resident not to call the Ombudsman, the Senior Helpline or IDPH, and may not monitor or prevent such calls. Residents may use a telephone, in private, at any reasonable time.

14. Monthly, the Administrator summarizes grievances (number, type, time to resolve, repeats) for the Quality Improvement committee. The committee identifies trends and opens an improvement project when needed. (See QI-01.)
15. The Administrator reviews every grievance in which retaliation is alleged, as a separate matter. Substantiated retaliation results in discipline and is reported to the governing body.
16. Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually. (See PER-06.)

responsibilities.duty: Serves as grievance officer; keeps the log; investigates or assigns investigation; responds in writing; prevents retaliation; reports trends to QI.
Accept complaints, document them the same day, pass them to the Administrator, and never discourage or retaliate.
Reviews grievance trends monthly or quarterly as set in QI-01 and tracks corrective actions.
Reviews summary grievance reports and acts on serious or repeated problems.

documentation: Grievance Forms
Grievance Log (date received, issue, investigator, date of response, resolution, satisfaction)
Written responses to complainants
Posted notice of the Senior Helpline and Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program
Signed contract showing the complaint process notice (C8)
Ombudsman visit log
QI meeting minutes reflecting grievance review

policies.category: Subpart F – Resident Rights (§ 295.6000–295.6030)
policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; all staff, volunteers, contractors and students who may see or hear resident information
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy of each resident and the confidentiality of resident information in any form, to limit access to those who need it, and to respond properly to requests for information and to any breach.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps resident information confidential. Access to resident records is limited to authorized staff who need the information to do their jobs. The agency releases information only with the resident's (or representative's) written authorization or as the law permits or requires. The agency applies the HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164) where it is a covered entity, and the administrator confirms and documents the agency's status. For example, the agency is a covered entity if it conducts standard electronic health care transactions, such as billing Medicaid through the Supportive Living Program. Where the agency is not a covered entity, it still follows the practices in this policy as its own standard. Other state and federal confidentiality laws that give greater protection to particular information (for example, mental health or substance use treatment records) are also followed. Residents also have the right to personal privacy in their rooms, in personal care and in their communications. Suspected breaches are reported internally at once and handled as set out below.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable health information about a resident, in any form (paper, electronic or oral), held by the agency.
A health care provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with standard transactions, a health plan, or a clearinghouse, as defined in 45 CFR Part 160.
An impermissible use or disclosure of PHI that compromises its security or privacy, unless a documented risk assessment shows a low probability that the information was compromised.
The least amount of PHI needed for the purpose of a use or disclosure.

procedures: 1. The Administrator determines whether the agency is a HIPAA covered entity (for example, whether it will bill Medicaid electronically). The Administrator documents the determination, with the date and reasons, and re-checks it whenever billing practices change and at each annual policy review.
2. The Administrator designates a Privacy Officer, who may be the Administrator, by name in writing. The name is given to all staff.

3. At hire, before any access to records, each employee, volunteer and contractor signs a confidentiality agreement and receives training on this policy. Refresher training is given annually. (See PER-06.)

4. The Administrator assigns record access by job role. Paper records are kept in a locked cabinet or room. Electronic records require individual log-ins and passwords that are not shared, and screens must be locked when staff step away.

5. Staff discuss resident information only where it cannot be overheard, and only with those who need it for care. Staff do not discuss residents in common areas, on social media, or with people outside the agency.

6. Staff do not post names, photographs or health information of residents in public places, on whiteboards visible to visitors, or on social media. A resident's written authorization is required before a photo or name is used publicly.

7. Release of information: the Privacy Officer releases information only on a signed authorization that names the person to receive it, the information to be released, the purpose, and an expiration date, or as the law permits (for example, to treating providers, to IDPH or the Ombudsman as authorized by law, or in a legally required report of abuse or neglect).

8. Staff confirm the identity of any caller or requester before releasing any information. Staff refer all requests from the media, attorneys, law enforcement and other outside parties to the Privacy Officer.

9. Requests by a resident or representative for a copy of the record, or for a copy of the assessment and service plan, are handled by the Privacy Officer promptly. The agency gives access as required by law and may charge only what the law allows.
10. The Privacy Officer keeps a log of disclosures that are not for treatment, payment or operations, and of all authorizations on file.
11. Records sent by fax, email or mail are sent only to verified recipients, using secure methods. Faxes carry a confidentiality cover sheet. Email containing PHI is encrypted.

12. A staff member who suspects a breach, such as a lost record, misdirected fax, stolen device or unauthorized access, reports it to the Privacy Officer immediately, and no later than the end of the shift.
13. The Privacy Officer investigates at once, limits further harm, and completes a documented risk assessment within 5 business days.

14. If the Privacy Officer determines a breach occurred and the agency is a covered entity, the agency notifies each affected resident (or representative) in writing without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery. The agency also meets the HIPAA requirements for notifying the federal Department of Health and Human Services and, for larger breaches, the media, as set out in 45 CFR Part 164.

15. The agency takes disciplinary action, up to termination, against any staff member who improperly accesses or discloses resident information. No resident is retaliated against for filing a privacy complaint.
16. The agency gives each resident at admission a Notice of Privacy Practices, if it is a covered entity, and obtains an acknowledgment of receipt.
17. Records are stored and disposed of as set out in REC-01. Paper is shredded and electronic media are wiped before disposal.

responsibilities.duty: Determines covered-entity status; designates the Privacy Officer; enforces sanctions; ensures training.
Handles authorizations, access requests, disclosure log, breach investigation and notification.
Access only the information needed for their duties; keep records secure; report suspected breaches promptly.
May review records, request corrections, authorize or revoke releases, and file privacy complaints.

documentation: Written covered-entity determination
Privacy Officer designation
Signed staff confidentiality agreements and training records
Signed authorizations for release
Disclosure log
Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgments (if applicable)
Breach reports, risk assessments and notifications
Access lists by job role

policies.category: Subpart F – Resident Rights (§ 295.6000–295.6030)
policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; all staff, applicants, residents, representatives and visitors
policies.purpose: To make sure applicants, residents and visitors are treated fairly and are not discriminated against, that people with disabilities receive reasonable accommodations, and that people with limited English proficiency or communication disabilities receive information in a way they can understand.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admission, services, discharge or treatment on the basis of race, color, national origin, ancestry, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age (apart from the age eligibility of the licensed program), disability, marital status, or any other characteristic protected by federal or state law. Admission decisions rest on the admission and retention criteria in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2000 and the agency's admission policies (RES-01 and RES-02), and not on any protected characteristic. The agency gives reasonable accommodations to people with disabilities, as the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12101 et seq.) requires. The agency provides interpreters or translated materials where needed so people can understand their rights, contract, service plan and care. Where the agency receives federal financial assistance (for example, Medicaid payments under the Supportive Living Program), it also complies with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 USC 2000d). The agency does not retaliate against anyone who asks for an accommodation or files a discrimination complaint.

definitions.definition: A change in rules, policies, practices, services or the physical setting that gives a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the services, unless it would impose an undue burden or fundamentally alter the service.
A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to take part in services without language help.
A person who is competent in both languages (or in sign language) and in interpreting, and who is impartial.
Items and services that allow effective communication with people with hearing, vision or speech disabilities, such as large print, sign language interpreters, or amplification.

procedures: 1. The Administrator designates a Civil Rights Coordinator (the Administrator unless otherwise assigned) who handles accommodation requests and discrimination complaints. The name and contact number are posted with the grievance notice. [PHONE]

2. The agency posts a nondiscrimination statement in the admission area and prints it in the resident handbook and on the establishment contract package. It tells people how to ask for help or file a complaint.

3. When any inquiry is made, the Administrator or designee applies the same criteria in RES-01 and RES-02 to all applicants. The Administrator records the specific criterion relied on in any decision not to admit, and the decision is reviewed by a second person where practical. Reasons may never include a protected characteristic.

4. At the pre-admission interview and at each reassessment, staff ask each applicant or resident whether he or she needs any accommodation, language assistance or alternate format. The answers are recorded in the record and in the service plan.

5. When an accommodation is requested, the Civil Rights Coordinator discusses it with the resident, decides within 5 business days if possible, and documents the request, the decision and any alternative offered. If the accommodation cannot be provided, the Coordinator explains why in writing and offers an alternative that meets the need.

6. Examples of accommodations include a service animal or assistance animal where permitted by law, grab bars and a roll-in shower, large-print menus and documents, adjusted meal times, alert systems for hearing loss, and help reading and signing documents. The Coordinator asks for documentation of the need only when the need is not obvious and only as the law allows.

7. Language access: the agency identifies the primary language of each applicant and resident at the first contact and records it. If the person cannot communicate well in English, staff arrange a qualified interpreter (in person, by phone or by video) for the assessment, contract signing, service planning, and any important discussion of care, rights, or consent.

8. The agency does not require a resident to supply his or her own interpreter. Staff may use a family member or friend only if the resident asks for that person after being told a free interpreter is available, and that choice is recorded. Staff do not use minor children as interpreters except in a true emergency.

9. The agency provides, or arranges, translated versions of the key documents (the contract's rights list, the grievance process and the notice of the Senior Helpline and Ombudsman) in the languages most often needed in the community served. Where a translation is not available, staff review the document through an interpreter and record that.

10. For residents who are deaf or hard of hearing, blind or low-vision, or who have a speech disability, staff use the auxiliary aid or service that the resident chooses, where available, such as sign language interpreter, written materials, large print, or a communication board.
11. The agency keeps a list of qualified interpreters, language lines and translation sources, with their contact details, at the front desk and in the staff office. Staff are trained to use them.

12. Staff treat all residents with respect and use the name and pronouns the resident prefers. They do not make jokes or comments about, or permit harassment based on, any protected characteristic. Residents may practice their culture and religion, subject to the safety of others. Staff report harassment to the Administrator.

13. Any person may file a discrimination complaint with the Civil Rights Coordinator, using the grievance process in RTS-04. The Coordinator investigates and responds in writing within 10 business days. The complaint form tells the person that he or she may also complain to the appropriate state or federal agency.

14. Where the agency participates in the Supportive Living Program or otherwise receives federal funds, the Administrator makes sure Title VI notices and language assistance requirements are met and keeps records showing compliance.

15. All staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually. (See PER-06.) The Administrator reviews accommodation and language access requests and complaints annually and reports results to the Quality Improvement committee.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures nondiscrimination in admission and care; approves accommodations; ensures interpreter resources and translated documents are available.
Receives and decides accommodation requests; investigates discrimination complaints; keeps records.
Asks about accommodation and language needs at assessment and records them in the service plan.
Treat all persons with respect, use interpreters and aids as required, and report discrimination.

documentation: Posted nondiscrimination statement
Admission decision records showing criteria applied
Accommodation request log and decisions
Primary language recorded in the resident record
Interpreter use records and list of interpreter and translation resources
Translated documents
Discrimination complaint records
Staff training records

policies.category: Subpart G – Resident and Establishment Records (§ 295.7000–295.7010)
policies.title: Resident Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; all staff who create, use, store or release resident and establishment records
policies.purpose: To make sure a complete, accurate, secure and accessible record is kept for every resident, that the documents a surveyor or the annual on-site reviewer may examine are available, and that records are kept for the required time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a record for every resident that includes the signed establishment contract, the comprehensive assessment, the service plan and the other documents listed below. The signed contract stays on the premises (C8). The pre-admission comprehensive assessment is completed by a physician, physician assistant or advanced practice registered nurse, and is repeated at least annually and on a significant change in condition (C1). The service plan is reviewed at least annually or when needs change (C1). On request, the resident or representative receives a copy of the latest assessment, any supplemental establishment assessment, and the service plan (C1). The agency keeps the documents that the annual on-site reviewer examines, as described in the contract's statement from IDPH on the annual on-site review process (C8). Incident reports are kept for one year and written drill evaluations are kept for one year. For all other records, retention periods follow the Department's rules on records. As the agency's own standard, resident records are kept for at least five years after discharge or death, or longer if a Department rule, other law, or an HFS requirement (if the agency participates in the Supportive Living Program) requires it. The administrator confirms the rule periods at each annual policy review. Records are kept confidential as set out in RTS-05 and 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164, where applicable.

definitions.definition: All documents, on paper or electronic, that concern an individual resident's admission, contract, assessments, service plan, care and services provided, incidents, medications, communications, and discharge.
The assessment of the resident's physical, cognitive and psychosocial condition completed by a physician, physician assistant or APRN before admission, and repeated as C1 requires.
Any additional assessment the agency itself performs, such as of nutrition, skin integrity or function, to plan services.
IDPH's annual review at the establishment, for which the agency must make records available.

procedures: 1. The Administrator designates a Records Custodian (the Resident Services Coordinator unless otherwise assigned) responsible for the organization, security and retention of all resident records.

2. At admission, the Records Custodian opens a record for each resident that holds, at minimum: the signed establishment contract and any addenda; identification and emergency contacts; the representative's authority documents; advance directives; the pre-admission comprehensive assessment from the physician, PA or APRN; any supplemental establishment assessment; the service plan; the medication list and physician orders; consents and authorizations; and the Negotiated Risk Agreement, if any.

3. The Records Custodian places the original signed contract in the record kept on the premises and gives a copy to the resident or representative. Contract changes are written and signed by both parties and filed with the contract. (See CON-01.)

4. The Resident Services Coordinator files each new or updated assessment and service plan within 3 business days of completion, with the date and the name and credentials of the person who completed it. The Coordinator checks that the annual reassessment and service plan review are done on time and flags any due within 30 days.

5. Staff record services provided, changes of condition, physician and family notifications, incidents, falls, skin findings, refusals of care, and medication events in the record. Entries are timely, factual, dated and signed or electronically authenticated with the staff member's name and title. Late entries are labeled as late. Errors are corrected by a single line with initials and date, not erased or covered.

6. On request, the Records Custodian gives the resident or representative a copy of the latest assessment, any supplemental establishment assessment, and the service plan, as C1 provides. The request and the date the copy was given are noted in the record.

7. Incident and accident reports are kept for one year from the date of the incident, and reports made to IDPH are filed with them (see INC-01). The agency keeps drill evaluations for one year from the drill date (see DIS-03). Where a longer period is needed for a pending claim or investigation, the record is held until the matter ends.

8. The Records Custodian keeps a current 'survey binder' or electronic folder that holds the documents the IDPH annual on-site reviewer may examine, including those described in the contract's on-site review statement, so they can be shown promptly. The Administrator checks the folder for completeness each quarter.

9. Active records are kept in a locked cabinet or room, or in an access-controlled electronic system with individual log-ins, audit trails and regular backups. Only authorized staff have access, as set out in RTS-05. Records are never left unattended in common areas.

10. Records may be kept in electronic form if they are readily available to staff on duty and to surveyors on demand, can be printed legibly, and are backed up securely. If the electronic system is down, staff use paper downtime forms and later transfer the information.

11. Records are made available to IDPH and other agencies with legal authority on request. The Administrator is notified at once of any request and logs what was given. Records are released to others only under RTS-05.

12. At discharge or death, the Records Custodian completes the record within 14 days, including the discharge summary or death entry, final accounting of funds (see CON-03) and the termination notice, if any (see TERM-01). The record is then closed and moved to secure archive storage.

13. Closed records are kept for the retention period stated in this policy, indexed by resident name and date of discharge so they can be retrieved. The Records Custodian keeps a retention and destruction log.

14. When the retention period ends and no legal hold applies, the Administrator approves destruction in writing. Paper records are shredded and electronic records are permanently erased. The log records the date and method of destruction.

15. If the agency closes or is sold, the Administrator makes arrangements to preserve and transfer resident records as set out in CLO-01 and as the law requires, and tells residents where records will be kept.

16. The Administrator audits a sample of at least 10 percent of active records each quarter for completeness, timeliness of assessments and service plan reviews, and legibility, and reports the results to the Quality Improvement committee. (See QI-01.)

responsibilities.duty: Is responsible for the record system, retention schedule and destruction approvals; keeps the survey binder current; audits records.
Opens, maintains, secures, retrieves and archives records; logs releases and destruction.
Files assessments and service plans on time; tracks annual due dates; provides copies on request.
Make accurate, timely, signed entries and protect the confidentiality of records.

Signed establishment contract kept on premises (C8)
Comprehensive assessments, supplemental assessments, service plans and review dates (C1)
Records of copies given to residents or representatives
Incident reports (kept one year) and written drill evaluations (kept one year)
Survey binder or folder for the annual on-site review
Records release and disclosure log
Record audit results
Retention and destruction log

policies.category: Subpart G – Resident and Establishment Records (§ 295.7000–295.7010)
policies.title: Required Reports to IDPH and Annual On-Site Review
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; Administrator, manager, governing body and staff who prepare or send reports to IDPH
policies.purpose: To make sure the agency sends every required report and notice to the Illinois Department of Public Health on time, files its license renewal on time, and is ready for IDPH's annual on-site review.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] makes all required reports to IDPH accurately and on time. Serious incidents are reported to IDPH within 24 hours by email to DPH.LTCAL@illinois.gov (see INC-01 for the definition of a reportable incident and the content of the report). Changes of manager are reported to IDPH within 10 working days, and the administrator confirms the current deadline in the Department's rules at each annual policy review. The renewal application and fee are filed 120 to 150 days before the license expires (C10). The agency may ask for a two-year renewal, but IDPH 'may' grant it only if, in the preceding 24 months, there was no Type 1 or Type 2 violation, no inspection with a finding of 10 or more Type 3 violations, and no admission or retention of a resident in violation of Section 75 (C10). The establishment contract includes a statement from IDPH on the annual on-site review process (C8), and the agency cooperates fully with that review.

definitions.definition: An event defined in INC-01 that must be reported to IDPH within 24 hours, such as a death or serious injury from an accident, abuse or neglect, or another event required by the rules.
IDPH's yearly review of the establishment, as described in the statement included in each establishment contract.
Classifications of violations by IDPH according to severity, used by the Department in survey findings and in deciding on renewal terms.
The agency's list of dates when reports, renewals and notices are due.

procedures: 1. The Administrator maintains a Regulatory Reporting Calendar that lists each recurring report and filing, including license renewal windows, the due date, the person responsible, and the date sent.

2. Serious incidents: when a serious incident occurs, the staff member in charge notifies the Administrator immediately. The Administrator or designee sends the report to IDPH by email at DPH.LTCAL@illinois.gov within 24 hours of the incident or of learning of it. The report includes the information required in INC-01. The sender keeps a copy of the email and any attachments.
3. If the Administrator cannot be reached, the senior staff member on duty sends the 24-hour report. The Administrator reviews it the next day and sends any follow-up information.

4. The Administrator follows up with IDPH as requested, sends any written summary or investigation findings, and records the case in the incident log. Incident reports are kept for one year (see REC-01).

5. Changes of manager: whenever a manager or director leaves or is replaced, or a new manager is hired, the Administrator or governing body sends IDPH written notice of the change within 10 working days. The notice names the new manager, gives the start date, and includes documents showing the qualifications in PER-05. The Administrator checks the current rule at each annual policy review to confirm the deadline.

6. If the manager's position becomes vacant, the governing body names an interim manager who meets the qualifications. The agency tells IDPH the interim manager's name in the same 10-working-day period and documents the plan to fill the position.

7. Renewal: the Administrator enters on the calendar the date 150 days and the date 120 days before the license expiration date. The renewal application and fee are prepared by day 150 and filed with IDPH no later than day 120 before expiration. The Administrator keeps proof of filing. (See APP-01.)

8. Two-year renewal: before filing, the Administrator reviews the preceding 24 months of survey findings and records of admissions and retentions to see whether a Type 1 or Type 2 violation, an inspection with 10 or more Type 3 violations, or an admission or retention in violation of Section 75 occurred. If none occurred, the agency may request a two-year renewal in writing. The agency understands that IDPH may grant, but is not required to grant, the request. If any of these occurred, the agency requests an annual renewal.

9. Other required reports: the Administrator also sends any other report or notice IDPH rules or the license require (for example, notices of closure, changes in ownership, or construction plan submissions). The Administrator follows the policies on those topics (see CLO-01, APP-01 and PP-01) and adds each due date to the calendar.

10. Annual on-site review: the Administrator keeps the survey binder or folder current, as set out in REC-01, so records are ready at any time. Every contract contains IDPH's statement on the annual on-site review process, and the Administrator explains it to residents and representatives when asked.

11. When IDPH arrives, staff greet the reviewers, ask for identification, and tell the Administrator or the highest-ranking manager on duty at once. If the Administrator is away, the designated manager receives the reviewers. Staff may not obstruct or delay entry.

12. The Administrator or designee accompanies the reviewers, makes requested records, staff and residents available as the reviewers direct, provides copies when asked, and keeps a log of documents provided. Staff answer questions truthfully. Staff do not alter or backdate any record.
13. At the exit meeting the Administrator listens to the findings, asks for clarification, and records the findings. The Administrator tells the governing body within 2 business days.

14. If IDPH issues a statement of violations, the Administrator prepares the written plan of correction within the time IDPH specifies, sends it on time, completes the corrections by the dates promised, and keeps evidence of correction. (See GOV-02.)

15. The Administrator reviews the reporting calendar quarterly and reports to the governing body on all reports made, renewal status, and any late or missed filings. Any late or missed report is investigated and corrected, and the cause is addressed through the Quality Improvement program. (See QI-01.)

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the reporting calendar; sends or supervises all reports to IDPH; files renewal on time; hosts the annual on-site review; sends plans of correction.
Notifies the Administrator of serious incidents at once and sends the 24-hour report if the Administrator cannot be reached.
Receives quarterly reporting summaries; notifies IDPH of manager changes in the Administrator's absence; funds renewal fees.
Keeps the survey binder and copies of all reports and proof of filing.
