policies.category: Subpart H – Food Service (§ 295.8000)
policies.title: Food Service and Therapeutic Diets
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment: all dietary, kitchen, direct care and management staff involved in meals, snacks, special diets or nutrition monitoring
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident receives safe, nutritious, appetizing food that fits his or her assessed needs, preferences and any ordered therapeutic diet, and that food service is staffed, supervised and sanitary as Subpart H requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides food service as required by the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act and Subpart H of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295 (§ 295.8000). Menu, diet and sanitation standards are applied as written in the current text of § 295.8000, and the Administrator verifies that text against the IDPH/JCAR current version at each annual policy review (see GOV-01). Under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000(h), staffing must be sufficient to cover food service if it is provided, and employees who work in food service must complete the initial health evaluation under Subpart C (§ 295.3030; see PER-07) before handling food. Nutrition needs are identified in the pre-admission comprehensive assessment and in reassessments completed by a physician, physician assistant or APRN under 210 ILCS 9/15, and are carried into the written service plan. IDPH may set more frequent nutrition assessments by rule, and [AGENCY NAME] will adopt any such schedule when it takes effect. Therapeutic diets are provided only on the written order of a licensed practitioner who may lawfully give it. Residents keep the right to choose among foods offered and to refuse food, and the agency documents refusals and notifies the resident's practitioner when a refusal affects health.

definitions.definition: A diet ordered by a physician, physician assistant or APRN to treat a medical condition, such as a consistent-carbohydrate, sodium-restricted, renal, texture-modified or thickened-liquid diet.

The review of a resident's weight, intake, appetite, swallowing, dental status, allergies, diet orders and food preferences, completed as part of the comprehensive assessment (210 ILCS 9/15) and at any additional interval IDPH sets by rule.
Any employee, including direct care staff, who prepares, handles, serves or stores food for residents.
Holding, cooling and reheating practices that keep potentially hazardous food in the safe ranges set by § 295.8000 and the local health authority.

procedures: Before opening and at each annual policy review, the Administrator reads the current text of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.8000 and updates the kitchen checklist, menu standards and sanitation log to match, and records the date and reviewer in the policy version log.

The Administrator designates a Food Service Supervisor, [FOOD SERVICE SUPERVISOR NAME], who is responsible for menus, ordering, food safety, kitchen cleaning and food service staff scheduling, and lists that duty in the job description (PER-03).

The Administrator builds food service coverage into the personnel schedule for every shift (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000(h) and (i)) so that meal preparation never depends on pulling direct care staff away from residents who need assistance (PER-01).

Before starting work, every food service employee completes the initial health evaluation described in PER-07. The Administrator keeps the evaluation in the employee file, and an employee with a symptom or condition that could spread through food is not assigned to food handling until cleared.

The Food Service Supervisor writes menus in advance, dates them and posts them where residents can see them. The menus offer variety, account for resident preferences and cultural or religious needs, and include the meals and snacks described in the resident contract (CON-01) and the service list in CARE-02.
The Food Service Supervisor keeps a record of the menu as actually served. Any substitution is noted on the menu record the same day.

During the pre-admission comprehensive assessment (CARE-01), the examining physician, physician assistant or APRN records diet needs, allergies, swallowing or chewing problems and any ordered therapeutic diet. The Administrator or designee transfers this information to the resident's service plan and to the kitchen diet list before the move-in date.

The kitchen keeps a current diet list showing each resident's name, allergies, texture and therapeutic diet orders. The Food Service Supervisor updates it within the same day of any new or changed order and removes discontinued orders.

A therapeutic diet is started only on a written or properly documented order from a physician, physician assistant or APRN. Staff do not start, change or stop a therapeutic diet on their own judgment. If an order is unclear, the Food Service Supervisor calls the practitioner for clarification and documents the call.

Direct care staff weigh each resident at admission and at least monthly, or more often if the service plan or an IDPH nutrition-assessment rule requires, and record the weight in the resident record. [AGENCY NAME] standard: a weight change of 5% or more in 30 days, a pattern of refusing meals, or new coughing or choking with meals is reported to the Administrator the same day and to the resident's practitioner under CARE-05.
Staff offer fluids throughout the day to residents at risk of dehydration, and the service plan names residents who need prompting or assistance to eat or drink.

Staff follow the safe food handling, hand-washing, cleaning and sanitizing, cold and hot holding, cooling, reheating and date-labelling practices in § 295.8000 and any local health department rules. The Food Service Supervisor keeps the daily refrigerator, freezer and (where used) dish-machine temperature log and reviews it weekly.

The Food Service Supervisor inspects food storage areas weekly, discards expired or unsafe items, and keeps chemicals stored separately from food. Pest sightings are reported to the Administrator the same day and handled under PP-02.

When a resident, representative or family member brings in food, staff advise on safe storage and, if the resident has a therapeutic diet, advise of the risks. Any resident-chosen deviation from a ordered diet is documented, the practitioner is notified, and a negotiated risk agreement is considered under NRA-01.

Resident or representative concerns about food are handled as complaints under RTS-04. The Administrator reviews food complaints, weight-loss trends and kitchen inspection findings at each quality improvement meeting (QI-01).
Kitchen sanitation logs, diet lists and menu records are filed as described under Documentation and retained according to REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Verifies current § 295.8000 requirements, assigns food service coverage in the personnel schedule, ensures health evaluations are complete, and reviews food service findings in quality improvement.
Writes and posts menus, keeps the diet list current, supervises food safety and sanitation, maintains temperature and cleaning logs, and reports problems the same day.
Completes the nutrition portion of the comprehensive assessment and gives written orders for any therapeutic diet.
Serve and assist at meals according to the service plan, offer fluids, record weights and intake as directed, and report refusals, choking or weight changes immediately.
Take part in setting food preferences and diet needs in the service plan and tell staff about allergies and changes in appetite.

documentation: Posted dated menus and menu-as-served records
Current resident diet list with allergies and therapeutic diet orders
Practitioner diet orders and clarification calls
Resident weight records and nutrition portion of each assessment and service plan
Refrigerator, freezer and dish-machine temperature logs
Kitchen cleaning and sanitation logs and storage inspection records
Food service employee health evaluations (employee file)
Food complaints and resulting corrective actions

policies.category: Subpart I – Physical Plant and Environmental Requirements (§ 295.9000–295.9040)
policies.title: Physical Plant, Units, Furnishings and Construction Plan Review
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment: the Administrator, owner or governing body, maintenance staff, and any contractor performing construction, remodeling or alteration
policies.purpose: To make sure the building, resident units and furnishings meet Subpart I of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295, that new construction and major alterations have IDPH-approved drawings before work begins, and that the building is accessible and safe for residents.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains its building, units and furnishings in compliance with Subpart I (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.9000–295.9040). The agency applies the standards in § 295.9000 (general), § 295.9005 (Units), § 295.9010 (assisted living establishments), § 295.9020 (shared housing establishments) and § 295.9030 (Furnishings), as they appear in the current rule text, and the Administrator verifies that text at each annual policy review. No new construction or major alteration begins until IDPH has approved the drawings in writing. IDPH reviews submitted drawings by issuing a completeness notice within 10 working days of receipt and approving or disapproving within 45 calendar days; the review does not start until any required fee is paid. IDPH Design and Construction performs the pre-licensure survey, and [AGENCY NAME] will not admit a resident until the building has passed that survey and the license is issued (APP-01). The agency also meets applicable Americans with Disabilities Act accessibility requirements for the building and common areas, and provides reasonable accommodation for residents and visitors with disabilities (RTS-06).

definitions.definition: The resident's living space as defined in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.9005, whose size, features and furnishing standards the agency checks against the current rule.

Any construction, renovation, addition or change in use or layout that requires IDPH review of drawings before work begins, as determined by IDPH. When in doubt, the Administrator asks IDPH in writing before starting.
IDPH's notice, due within 10 working days of receiving plans, saying whether the submission is complete.
The IDPH section that reviews construction drawings and conducts the Life Safety Code and physical plant survey before licensure.

procedures: Before purchasing, leasing or renovating a building, the owner or governing body gives the Administrator the proposed floor plans so the Administrator can compare them with §§ 295.9000–295.9040 and the type of establishment (assisted living or shared housing).

The Administrator keeps a physical plant compliance checklist built from §§ 295.9000, 295.9005, 295.9010 (assisted living), 295.9020 (shared housing) and 295.9030, and updates it against the current rule text each year.
For new construction or major alteration, the Administrator submits drawings and any required fee to IDPH Design and Construction and records the date received.
The Administrator tracks the IDPH completeness notice (due within 10 working days of receipt) and answers any request for missing information within [NUMBER] business days.
The Administrator tracks the IDPH decision date (45 calendar days from receipt of a complete submission) and does not allow construction to begin until written approval is in hand.
If IDPH disapproves the drawings, the Administrator, with the architect, corrects and resubmits them and keeps all correspondence in the physical plant file.
The Administrator tells contractors in writing that work must follow the approved drawings, and any change from them is submitted to IDPH for approval before it is built.

Before the pre-licensure survey, the Administrator walks the building with the checklist, confirms every unit and common area, and corrects deficiencies. The Administrator then schedules the IDPH Design and Construction survey as part of the licensing process (APP-01).
The Administrator accompanies IDPH surveyors on the physical plant survey, records any findings, and submits a written plan of correction within the time IDPH gives.

Before each new admission, maintenance staff inspect the assigned unit, verify that it is clean, in good repair and furnished or arranged as the contract (CON-01) promises, and sign the unit readiness checklist.

Where the contract says the establishment supplies furnishings, maintenance staff confirm that furnishings meet § 295.9030 and are safe, clean and in good repair. Where a resident brings his or her own furnishings, the Administrator checks that they do not block egress or create hazards (PP-03).

The Administrator reviews building and common areas at least annually for ADA accessibility (entrances, routes, restrooms, signage, door hardware) and records barriers and a dated plan to remove them. Reasonable modification requests from residents are handled under RTS-06.
Maintenance staff walk the building at least monthly and record repairs needed. Items affecting resident safety are corrected immediately or the area is closed off until repaired.
Before any later remodeling, change in the number of units, or change in use of space, the Administrator asks IDPH in writing whether drawings must be submitted, and keeps the answer in the file.
The Administrator keeps approved drawings, IDPH approval letters, survey reports and plans of correction for the life of the building, and keeps copies available for surveyors.

responsibilities.duty: Provides funding and authority for compliant construction, does not allow work to start without IDPH approval, and keeps the building in licensable condition.
Maintains the compliance checklist, submits drawings and fees, tracks IDPH deadlines, coordinates surveys and submits plans of correction.
Inspects units before admission, performs monthly walk-throughs, makes repairs, and follows approved drawings for any work.
Prepare drawings that meet Subpart I and ADA, and build only what IDPH has approved.

documentation: Physical plant compliance checklist with annual review dates
Submitted drawings, fee receipt, IDPH completeness notice and approval or disapproval letters
IDPH Design and Construction survey reports and plans of correction
Unit readiness checklists for each admission
Monthly building walk-through and repair records
ADA accessibility review and barrier-removal plan
Written IDPH inquiries and answers about alterations

policies.category: Subpart I – Physical Plant and Environmental Requirements (§ 295.9000–295.9040)
policies.title: Environmental Requirements, Housekeeping, Laundry and Maintenance
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment: housekeeping, laundry, maintenance, direct care staff and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To keep the building clean, safe, comfortable and in good repair, to protect residents and employees from infection and bloodborne pathogen exposure, and to make sure environmental services are staffed as required.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] meets the environmental requirements of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.9040 as written in the current rule text, which the Administrator verifies at each annual policy review. Staffing must cover environmental services, which are among the services staffing must address under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000(h)(5), and the personnel schedule includes housekeeping, laundry and maintenance coverage (PER-01). Indoor temperatures and heat index are monitored in connection with the temperature table (Table A) in Part 295, with actions as set out in DIS-02. Employees with occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious material are protected under the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030. The agency keeps a preventive maintenance log showing that building systems, equipment and safety devices are inspected and serviced on a set schedule.

definitions.definition: A measure combining air temperature and humidity that is monitored in resident living areas as tied to Table A and the actions in DIS-02.
A dated record of scheduled inspection, testing, servicing and repair of building systems and equipment.
The written plan required by 29 CFR 1910.1030 identifying jobs with exposure to blood or other potentially infectious material and the protective measures used.
Treating all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious and using barriers and hand hygiene accordingly.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a housekeeping schedule assigning each resident unit and common area a cleaning frequency, and a named person is responsible for each shift.

Housekeeping staff clean units on the posted schedule and whenever soiled, using products labelled for the task. They store chemicals in a locked or restricted area and keep safety data sheets available for staff.

The Administrator includes housekeeping, laundry and maintenance coverage in the personnel schedule for each week (295.3000(h)(5) and (i)). Direct care staff are not pulled from resident care to cover environmental tasks unless the schedule shows enough remaining staff.

Laundry staff separate soiled linen from clean at the point of use, handle soiled linen with gloves, do not shake it, wash it in the manner the Administrator sets out in the laundry procedure, and keep clean and soiled linen paths separate. Resident personal laundry is labelled and returned to the correct resident.

The Administrator writes an exposure control plan under 29 CFR 1910.1030, identifies the positions with exposure, offers hepatitis B vaccination at no cost to employees with exposure, supplies gloves and personal protective equipment, and updates the plan at least annually.

Sharps are placed in puncture-resistant containers, and regulated waste is bagged, labelled and disposed of through a licensed waste carrier. Staff who have an exposure incident report it at once to the Administrator, who arranges immediate evaluation and records the incident.

Maintenance staff keep the preventive maintenance log for heating, cooling, hot water, plumbing, electrical, elevators (if any), call or alert systems, generators (if any), kitchen and laundry equipment, and fire safety equipment (see PP-03), entering each task by date and initials.

Maintenance staff monitor indoor temperature and heat index in resident areas using the thermometers and schedule set by the Administrator. When readings reach the Table A levels, they follow DIS-02, and they log the reading, time and action taken.

The Administrator posts a method for residents and staff to report a maintenance problem. A work order is opened for every report and logged with the date received, the person assigned and the date completed.

Hazards affecting resident safety, such as a leak, broken door lock, loss of heat or hot water, or electrical fault, are repaired immediately or the affected area is closed, and the Administrator is told at once. Prolonged loss of services is handled under DIS-01.
The Administrator arranges pest control by a licensed contractor on a regular schedule and for any sighting, and keeps the service reports.

Maintenance staff check water temperatures at resident-accessible fixtures at least monthly, record them, and correct any reading outside the limits the Administrator has set in line with 295.9040 and local code.
Staff keep exits, corridors and common areas free of clutter and keep floors dry or marked when wet to prevent falls (CARE-06).
The Administrator reviews the work order log, maintenance log and environmental findings at each quality improvement meeting (QI-01) and acts on repeat problems.

The Administrator trains housekeeping, laundry and maintenance staff at orientation and annually on infection control, bloodborne pathogens, chemical safety and this policy (PER-06), and records the training in the employee file.

responsibilities.duty: Verifies § 295.9040 requirements, schedules environmental staff, maintains the exposure control plan, reviews maintenance and temperature logs, and ensures corrective action.
Keeps the preventive maintenance log, monitors temperature and heat index, completes work orders and arranges outside contractors.
Clean and launder according to schedule and infection control practice, use protective equipment, and report hazards and exposures.
Use universal precautions, report maintenance and safety problems immediately, and report any exposure incident.

Laundry procedure and training record
Exposure control plan, hepatitis B vaccine offers or declinations, and exposure incident reports
Preventive maintenance log
Temperature and heat index readings with actions taken
Work order log
Pest control service reports
Water temperature checks
Environmental staff training records

policies.category: Subpart I – Physical Plant and Environmental Requirements (§ 295.9000–295.9040)
policies.title: Fire Safety, Life Safety Code and Evacuation
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment: all employees, the Administrator, maintenance staff, residents and visitors
policies.purpose: To protect residents, staff and visitors from fire and related emergencies by keeping fire protection systems working, staffing enough awake employees to move residents to safety, and training everyone on evacuation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] complies with the Life Safety Code requirements enforced by IDPH, whose Design and Construction Section conducts the Life Safety Code survey before licensure (see PP-01 and APP-01). Under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000(h)(6), staffing must cover evacuation of residents, and under 295.3000(j) awake staff are required for residents who cannot self-move to safety; the agency schedules enough awake staff on every shift to move impaired residents to safety (PER-01 and PER-02). Fire alarm, detection, suppression and related systems are tested, serviced and documented, and inspection tags are kept current. Because system requirements depend on the building and the occupancy classification, the Administrator confirms the required systems and test frequencies with IDPH and the local fire authority before opening and whenever the building or its use changes, and records the answer.

definitions.definition: The fire and life safety standards adopted for this occupancy and enforced by IDPH Design and Construction and local fire authorities, applied as confirmed by IDPH.
A resident who cannot move to safety without help because of physical, cognitive or other limitation, as identified in the comprehensive assessment and service plan.
Staff who are on duty, on site and awake, and who are not counted in other roles that prevent them from helping evacuate residents.
Moving residents to a safe area in the building or to the outside as set out in the evacuation plan.

procedures: Before opening, the Administrator asks IDPH Design and Construction and the local fire authority in writing which fire alarm, detection, sprinkler, extinguisher, emergency lighting and exit requirements apply, and records the answers and dates in the fire safety file.
The Administrator completes the IDPH Life Safety Code survey process before licensure (PP-01, APP-01) and corrects any deficiency within the time IDPH gives.

Maintenance staff or a qualified contractor test the fire alarm system, smoke and heat detection, extinguishers, emergency lighting, exit signs and any sprinkler system at the frequency required by the code or authority confirmed above, and record the date, tester, result and any repair.
Maintenance staff verify at least monthly that inspection tags on extinguishers and systems are present and current, and arrange renewals before expiration.
Maintenance staff check daily or on each shift walk-through that exits, corridors and stairways are unobstructed, exit doors operate, and fire doors are not propped open.

The Administrator writes a fire and evacuation plan for the building that shows exits, routes, assembly points, how each unit is evacuated, who calls 911, and how residents who need help are moved. It is posted in common areas and reviewed annually.

During the pre-admission assessment and each reassessment (CARE-01), the examining practitioner and Administrator identify each resident's evacuation ability. The service plan notes needed help, and the Administrator keeps a current evacuation list that identifies residents who cannot self-move to safety.

Using the evacuation list, the Administrator schedules enough awake staff on every shift, including nights, to move impaired residents to safety (295.3000(h)(6) and (j)), and records the staffing in the personnel schedule (PER-01, PER-02).

In a fire alarm or fire, staff follow the fire plan: remove anyone in immediate danger, close doors, activate the alarm, call 911, evacuate or relocate residents as the plan directs, account for every resident using the census, and remain with residents at the assembly point.

New employees are trained on the fire plan, alarm pull stations, extinguisher use, and evacuation techniques during orientation before working alone (PER-06). All employees repeat the training at least annually.
The agency conducts fire and evacuation drills on all shifts as DIS-03 sets out, and the Administrator completes a written evaluation of each drill, correcting any problem found.

Staff report any alarm malfunction, disabled system, or hazard to the Administrator immediately. If a system is out of service, the Administrator notifies the local fire authority as required, starts interim safety measures such as a fire watch, and documents them until the system is restored.

Smoking, candles, space heaters and cooking equipment are controlled as set out in DL-02 and unit rules, and the Administrator checks resident-owned appliances and furnishings for fire hazards at admission (PP-01).

After any fire, near miss or alarm activation, the Administrator reviews the response with staff within [NUMBER] business days, reports any incident that meets IDPH reporting criteria (INC-01), and updates the plan if needed.
The Administrator keeps all test records, tags, drill evaluations, fire authority correspondence and survey reports for the time stated in REC-01 and has them available for surveyors.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms fire system requirements with authorities, maintains the fire and evacuation plan and list, schedules enough awake staff, and reviews tests and drills.
Tests and services fire systems, keeps tags current, checks exits, and maintains testing records.
Know the fire plan, move residents to safety, account for every resident and report hazards.

responsibilities.role: Local Fire Authority / IDPH Design and Construction
responsibilities.duty: Advise on and inspect for Life Safety Code compliance.

documentation: Written confirmation of applicable fire system requirements from IDPH and the local fire authority
Fire alarm, detection, extinguisher, emergency lighting and sprinkler test and service records and current tags
Fire and evacuation plan and the current evacuation list
Training records on fire safety and evacuation
Drill records and written evaluations (DIS-03)
Impairment, fire watch and incident records

policies.category: Governance and Administration
policies.title: Governing Body, Administrator Responsibilities and Policy Review
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment: licensee, owners or governing body, Administrator / Director and management staff
policies.purpose: To define who is responsible for operating [AGENCY NAME] lawfully, to ensure a qualified full-time director is in place, and to keep this Policy & Procedure Manual current with the Act, Part 295 and changes in law.
policies.policy: No one may establish, operate, maintain or offer an assisted living or shared housing establishment without an IDPH license (210 ILCS 9/25). The licensee, [AGENCY NAME], through its governing body, is responsible for compliance with the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act (210 ILCS 9) and with 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295 (Subparts A through I). A license lasts one year, states the physical location with issue and expiration dates, and is not transferable (210 ILCS 9/35). The agency employs a full-time director/manager who is at least 21 years old with a high school diploma or equivalent and qualifying experience, and who completes at least 20 hours of training every 2 years as a condition of licensure (210 ILCS 9/35; see PER-05). The governing body gives the Administrator the authority and resources to run the establishment, keeps staffing sufficient in number and skill for the 24-hour scheduled and unscheduled needs of residents, and requires that all employees meet the Health Care Worker Background Check Act (PER-04). The Administrator reviews every policy in this manual at least annually and whenever a law or rule changes, including after Public Act 104-0589, and keeps a version log.

definitions.definition: The owner, board, members or managers of the licensee who hold ultimate legal responsibility for the establishment.
The full-time manager named in the license file who is responsible for daily operation and who meets 210 ILCS 9/35 qualifications.
A record of each policy's number, revision date, change made, reviewer and approval.

The 2025–2026 amendment to the Act, reported effective July 24, 2026 (the Administrator confirms the effective date against the Public Act text), which among other changes requires the pre-admission comprehensive assessment to be completed by a physician, physician assistant or APRN.

procedures: Before offering services, the governing body confirms in writing that the establishment is licensed and the license shows the correct physical location and dates (210 ILCS 9/25 and 9/35), and no one admits residents or advertises services before that.
The governing body adopts this manual by signed resolution or minutes, names [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] as Administrator/Director, and records the date.

The governing body meets at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., quarterly] and reviews census, staffing, incidents, complaints, survey results, quality improvement reports (QI-01), and finances as they affect resident care, and keeps minutes.

The Administrator verifies and keeps proof that the director meets the age, education and experience qualifications of 210 ILCS 9/35, and tracks the 20 hours of training every 2 years in the director's file (PER-05).

The Administrator tells IDPH of any change of manager as PER-05 requires, and the governing body names an interim responsible person with the same qualifications when the director is absent for an extended period.

The Administrator ensures that staffing is sufficient in number and skill for 24-hour scheduled and unscheduled needs and reviews the personnel schedule against resident acuity at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., monthly] (PER-01).

The Administrator ensures that every employee subject to the Health Care Worker Background Check Act has met it before working alone with residents (PER-04) and that the Alzheimer's/dementia special care disclosure document is filed with IDPH if the establishment offers a dementia program (CARE-04).

The Administrator reviews each policy in this manual at least once every 12 months, compares it with the current Act, 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295 and IDPH guidance, and records the review date and reviewer in the version log.

Whenever a law or rule changes, the Administrator reviews affected policies within [NUMBER] days of learning of the change. For Public Act 104-0589, the Administrator confirms the effective date and revises admission, assessment and service plan policies (RES-01, CARE-01) before the effective date.
The Administrator drafts each revision with the version number, date and a short summary of changes, obtains governing body approval for substantive changes, and issues the revised policy to staff.
The Administrator trains staff on revised policies within [NUMBER] days of adoption, collects signed acknowledgments, and removes outdated copies from circulation while keeping an archive.
The Administrator checks that the contract form, resident rights notice and other resident-facing documents match the current policies and law (CON-01, RTS-01).
The Administrator keeps a copy of the Act and 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295 (or a link to current text) available to managers and surveyors.
The Administrator reports to the governing body at each meeting on survey results, civil penalties, complaints and corrective actions (GOV-02).
The Administrator keeps the current manual, version log, board minutes and approvals on site and available for IDPH on request.

responsibilities.duty: Holds legal responsibility for compliance, approves policies, appoints a qualified full-time director, provides resources and reviews performance.
Manages daily operations, keeps this manual current, ensures staffing, training and background checks, and reports to the governing body.
Apply policies in their areas, tell the Administrator when a policy does not work in practice, and train staff on revisions.
Read and follow policies, sign acknowledgments when policies change, and report conflicts or gaps.

documentation: Current IDPH license, posted as APP-01 requires
Governing body adoption resolution and meeting minutes
Director qualifications and 20-hour training record
Policy & Procedure Manual with version log and annual review sign-off
Records of rule-change reviews, including P.A. 104-0589
Staff policy-training acknowledgments
Archive of superseded policies

policies.category: Governance and Administration
policies.title: Regulatory Compliance, Surveys, Civil Penalties and Corporate Compliance
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment: governing body, Administrator, all managers and employees
policies.purpose: To prevent violations, respond properly to IDPH inspections and complaints, limit exposure to civil penalties, protect eligibility for license renewal, and maintain an internal compliance program with accurate billing.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] operates only under a valid IDPH license (210 ILCS 9/25) and complies with the Act and 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295. IDPH may assess a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation, and each day a violation continues is a separate violation (210 ILCS 9/135). A penalty of up to $3,000 per day may be assessed for caring for a resident who exceeds the care needs defined in the Act, so the agency does not admit or retain residents beyond those limits (RES-01, RES-02, TERM-01). Repeated technical infractions within a calendar year may become a Type 3 violation, and IDPH may hold hearings on appeals. A violation history also affects renewal: a license is renewed annually, with the application filed 120 to 150 days before expiration, and IDPH may grant a 2-year renewal at the licensee's request only if, in the preceding 24 months, there was no Type 1 or Type 2 violation, no inspection with 10 or more Type 3 violations, and no admission or retention of a resident in violation of Section 75 (210 ILCS 9/45). The agency runs an internal compliance program with self-audits, corrective action, a staff reporting channel without retaliation, and billing and fee practices that match the resident contract (CON-01, CON-02).

definitions.definition: The more serious violation classes under the Act, whose presence in the preceding 24 months bars a 2-year renewal (210 ILCS 9/45).
A less serious violation class. Ten or more at one inspection, or repeated technical infractions within a calendar year, have consequences for renewal and penalties.
The written response to cited violations describing how and when each will be corrected.
The agency's internal system of self-audit, training, reporting, discipline and correction used to prevent and detect violations.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a compliance calendar showing the license expiration date, the renewal filing window (120 to 150 days before expiration, 210 ILCS 9/45), training due dates, drill dates and other recurring deadlines, and reviews it at least monthly.
The Administrator starts the renewal file at least [NUMBER] days before the filing window opens and files the renewal application and fee within the 120 to 150 day window (APP-01).

Before deciding whether to request a 2-year renewal, the Administrator reviews the preceding 24 months of survey reports for any Type 1 or Type 2 violation, any inspection with 10 or more Type 3 violations, and any admission or retention in violation of Section 75, and records the finding. If any exist, the agency files for annual renewal only.

At least [FREQUENCY, e.g., quarterly], the Administrator performs a self-audit against 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295 using a checklist covering assessments, service plans, contracts, personnel files, background checks, training, medications, drills, physical plant and records, and records the results.
Every deficiency found in a self-audit is assigned an owner and a due date. The Administrator verifies correction and reports open items to the governing body (GOV-01).

Before each admission and each reassessment, the Administrator or designee confirms the resident does not exceed the care needs the Act defines and is not excluded under RES-01 and RES-02. If the resident's needs exceed those limits, the Administrator starts the lawful discharge process in TERM-01 without delay, since each day of retention may be a separate violation.

Employees treat IDPH surveyors and investigators courteously. The Administrator or senior person on duty greets them, notifies the Administrator immediately, gives them access to residents, staff, records and areas, and does not alter, backfill or destroy records.
The Administrator keeps a log of every survey, complaint investigation and visit, including dates, scope and who attended, and takes notes at the exit conference.

The Administrator reviews the written survey report on receipt, files a plan of correction within the time IDPH specifies, assigns owners and dates for every cited item, and follows up until corrected and documented.

When IDPH proposes a civil penalty or other action, the Administrator tells the governing body at once, reviews the facts, and decides whether to correct, pay or appeal. Any hearing request is filed within the time stated in IDPH's notice and handled with counsel as the governing body directs.

The Administrator tracks technical infractions of the same kind during the calendar year. If the same infraction is cited more than once, the Administrator performs a root-cause review and training to prevent it from becoming a Type 3 violation.

Billing and fees follow the signed contract exactly (CON-01, CON-02). The Administrator audits a sample of resident invoices, deposits and refunds at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., quarterly] to confirm charges match contract terms, notice of fee changes was given, and no resident is charged for services not provided.

Any employee may report a suspected violation or billing error to the Administrator, or to [GOVERNING BODY CONTACT] if the concern involves the Administrator, in person or in writing, without fear of retaliation. The agency investigates each report, documents the result and discipline or correction, and tells the reporter that it was reviewed.
Employees are trained on this policy and the compliance program at orientation and annually (PER-06), and managers are trained on survey readiness.
Reports required by IDPH are made on time under INC-01 and REC-02, and the Administrator reviews the reporting log monthly.
The Administrator reports survey results, penalties, self-audit trends and corrective action status to the governing body at each meeting and to the quality improvement committee (QI-01).

responsibilities.duty: Oversees compliance, decides on appeals and penalties, and provides resources for correction.
Maintains the compliance calendar, self-audits, survey responses, renewal eligibility review, billing audits and the reporting channel.
Correct deficiencies in their areas by the due date and train staff on cited issues.
Follow regulations and policies, cooperate with surveyors, never alter records, and report suspected violations.

documentation: Compliance calendar and renewal file with 24-month violation review
Quarterly self-audit checklists and corrective action tracker
Survey, complaint investigation and visitor log with reports, exit conference notes and plans of correction
Civil penalty notices, appeal filings and outcomes
Billing and fee audit records
Employee compliance reports and investigation results
Compliance training records

policies.category: Governance and Administration
policies.title: Supportive Living Program Participation (if applicable)
policies.applies_to: Only if [AGENCY NAME] is separately approved and certified by HFS as a Supportive Living Program provider under 89 Ill. Adm. Code 146. Private-pay-only operations omit this policy.
policies.purpose: To state how [AGENCY NAME] describes Medicaid payment accurately to applicants and residents, and, if the site is approved and certified by the Illinois Department of Healthcare and Family Services (HFS), how it participates in the Supportive Living Program (SLP) without weakening its IDPH licensure duties or resident rights.
policies.policy: Medicaid does not pay for services in an assisted living or shared housing establishment licensed by IDPH. The establishment contract must say so (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2030, C8). [AGENCY NAME] will not state or imply that Medicaid pays for care, and will not admit a resident on the expectation of Medicaid payment, unless and until HFS has separately approved and certified this site under 89 Ill. Adm. Code 146 (C15). If HFS certifies the site, [AGENCY NAME] will follow the HFS program rules, the person-centered and home- and community-based setting requirements of 42 CFR 441.301(c), and all IDPH licensure requirements. Where the two sets of rules differ, the Administrator will follow the stricter rule and confirm the point with HFS or IDPH in writing. Where the site is private-pay only, this policy stays in the manual only as a reference. The Governing Body will confirm in writing each year that the site's Medicaid status is correctly stated in marketing materials and in the contract.

definitions.definition: The HFS Medicaid home- and community-based services program, operated under a 1915(c) waiver and 89 Ill. Adm. Code 146, that pays for services to eligible residents only in sites HFS has approved and certified.
Separate written approval by HFS that allows a site to take part in the SLP. An IDPH license alone does not give it.
An IDPH-licensed establishment that has no HFS approval or certification and receives no Medicaid payment.
An SLP site HFS recognizes for dementia care, paid at a higher per diem (150% of the regular SLP per diem under the HFS schedule in effect).

The monthly housing and meal amount the SLP resident pays. HFS sets the amounts, which differ for single and double occupancy and change by year (2026: $874.00 single, $625.50 double, effective 2026-01-01; verify the current schedule).

procedures: Before the license application is filed, the Administrator and Governing Body decide in writing whether [AGENCY NAME] will seek SLP participation or remain private-pay only. The decision is recorded in Governing Body minutes.

If the site stays private-pay only, the Administrator confirms that the contract (CON-01) contains the required statement that Medicaid does not pay for services, and that the admission staff script and marketing materials say the same.

If the site seeks SLP participation, the Administrator contacts HFS (1-844-528-8444; HFS.SLF@illinois.gov) to get the current application requirements, the provider approval process and the certification timeline. The contact date and reference are logged.
The Administrator completes Medicaid provider enrollment through HFS IMPACT, and the Governing Body signs the HFS application materials.
No resident is admitted as an SLP resident, and no SLP payment is billed, until HFS gives written certification. A copy is filed in the Administrator's regulatory binder.

After certification, the Administrator adds HFS contact information, the SLP admission pathway and the room and board schedule to the admission packet. The Administrator checks that these still match the current HFS schedule at each January review.
The Admissions Coordinator tells every applicant, before the contract is signed, whether the site is private pay only or HFS-certified, and records that disclosure in the admission file.

For SLP residents, the Admissions Coordinator confirms Medicaid eligibility and the HFS assessment and eligibility steps before admission. The IDPH admission criteria in RES-01, RES-02 and CARE-01 still apply to every applicant.

The Service Plan for each SLP resident is person-centered and records the resident's own choices about services, roommate, daily schedule, visitors and use of their unit. This is the standard in 42 CFR 441.301(c).

The Administrator checks that no house rule limits an SLP resident's privacy, visitors, choice of activities or access to the community beyond what the resident's written risk agreement or service plan supports (RTS-01, ESP-01, NRA-01).
Room and board is billed to the SLP resident only at the HFS-approved amount. Any other charge must be a service the resident chose and that the contract allows (CON-02).
The Business Office keeps SLP claims and billing records apart from private-pay records, and the Administrator reviews them monthly for accuracy.
The Administrator reports changes of ownership, administrator, capacity or program to HFS and to IDPH within the timeframes each agency requires, and logs each notice.
HFS or IDPH survey findings affecting SLP status go to the Governing Body within five business days. The Administrator submits corrective action plans by the agency's due date (GOV-02).
The QI Committee reviews SLP-specific indicators each quarter, including resident choice, grievances, transfers and discharges (QI-01).

If HFS certification is denied, suspended or ends, the Administrator notifies affected residents in writing within one business day of the decision and starts relocation or payment-change planning with each resident and representative in line with TERM-01.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether to seek SLP participation, signs HFS applications, and reviews SLP compliance at least annually.
Contacts HFS, maintains certification, ensures accurate Medicaid disclosures, and reports program changes to HFS and IDPH.
Gives the private-pay or HFS-certified disclosure before contract signing and checks eligibility steps for SLP applicants.
Bills only HFS-approved amounts and keeps SLP records separate.
Writes person-centered service plans that reflect resident choice.
Reviews SLP indicators each quarter and recommends corrective actions.

documentation: Governing Body minutes recording the private-pay or SLP decision
HFS correspondence log, application, certification letter and enrollment confirmation
Signed disclosure of payment status in each admission file
Annual written check of marketing materials and contract Medicaid statement
SLP billing and room and board records
HFS and IDPH survey reports and corrective action plans

policies.category: Safety and Protection
policies.title: Elopement and Missing Resident
policies.applies_to: All residents and staff of [AGENCY NAME], including any special dementia program. Applies to both assisted living and shared housing operations.
policies.purpose: To prevent residents from leaving the building unsafely, to find any missing resident quickly, and to meet the wandering and evacuation safety duties that apply to dementia programs under 210 ILCS 9/150.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will assess each resident's risk of wandering and elopement before admission and at each reassessment, plan for that risk, and keep staff awake and able to supervise at all times (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000, C7). Residents are not confined. Any individual safety measure must be agreed with the resident or representative and recorded in the service plan or a negotiated risk agreement (SAF-02, NRA-01). Where [AGENCY NAME] offers a special dementia program, this policy serves as its written wandering and evacuation safety policy under 210 ILCS 9/150 (C5), and the program will have emergency procedures and staffing patterns suited to residents who wander. A resident is treated as missing as soon as staff cannot account for the resident and the resident is not known to be off premises with permission. A missing resident event that results in harm is a serious incident and is reported to IDPH within 24 hours under INC-01. A missing resident drill is held at the intervals required by DIS-03.

definitions.definition: A resident leaving the building or grounds without staff knowing, in a way that puts the resident at risk.
A resident whose location is unknown to staff and who is not known to be off premises with permission.
Aimless or purposeful movement, often by a resident with cognitive impairment, that may lead the resident into unsafe areas or out of the building.
The agency's overhead or radio alert that starts the search.
A program [AGENCY NAME] discloses to IDPH and residents as a dementia-specific offering (see CARE-04).

procedures: Before admission, the assessing clinician records each applicant's history of wandering, exit-seeking, getting lost, or leaving without notice, using the assessment in CARE-01. Findings are on the Service Plan.

The Service Plan Coordinator writes individual interventions for residents at risk, such as increased checks, escorted walks, structured activities, a current photograph on file, and a note about habits and likely destinations. The resident or representative is involved in that planning.
The Administrator keeps a current photograph and description of each at-risk resident in a sealed binder at [LOCATION OF BINDER] so it can be handed to responders at once.
Direct care staff learn each at-risk resident's identity and plan at orientation and at each shift report. The charge person assigns checks and records them on the shift log.
Staff schedules always provide at least one staff member awake, on duty and on site (assisted living), or on site (shared housing), and enough staff to watch residents at risk (PER-01, PER-02).
Exit doors and alerts: the Maintenance Director tests door alarms or other alert devices weekly and records the test. A device may not trap residents or block evacuation, and must comply with PP-03.
When a staff member cannot find a resident, that staff member calls the missing resident alert at once and tells the charge person. Nobody waits to confirm.

Within the first minutes, staff check the resident's room, bathrooms, common areas, other residents' rooms, laundry, kitchen, storage, stairwells, outdoor areas and vehicles, working in assigned zones. One staff member stays at the main entrance.

The charge person starts a timed log. If the resident is not found within 15 minutes, the charge person calls 911, gives the resident's description and last known location, and calls the Administrator or on-call manager at [PHONE].

The Administrator or on-call manager notifies the resident's representative and any essential support person by phone as soon as the resident is declared missing, and the resident's physician as needed (CARE-05).

When the resident is found, staff assess the resident for injury, dehydration, cold or heat exposure and distress, and call 911 if there is any concern. The physician is notified and the resident is monitored closely for at least 72 hours.

If the resident is harmed because of the event, the Administrator reports it to IDPH as a serious incident within 24 hours, following INC-01. The Administrator also considers whether neglect reporting under RTS-02 applies.

The charge person completes the incident report before the end of the shift. The Administrator completes a review within three business days to find the cause, such as an unlocked door, staffing gap or plan failure.

The Service Plan Coordinator updates the resident's Service Plan and any risk agreement within five business days and tells the family. If the resident's needs now exceed what [AGENCY NAME] can provide, the Administrator starts the process in RES-01 and TERM-01.
A missing resident drill is held on a rotation covering all shifts and evaluated in writing as required by DIS-03. Gaps found are corrected and the correction is recorded.
The QI Committee reviews every missing resident event and every drill evaluation each quarter (QI-01).

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy, reviews each event, reports serious incidents to IDPH within 24 hours, and ensures staffing and drills.
Assesses elopement risk and writes and updates resident-specific interventions.
Assigns checks, directs the search, calls 911 when needed and starts the timed log.
Know at-risk residents, perform assigned checks and sound the alert at once.
Tests alarms and exits weekly and keeps them compliant with life safety rules.
Reviews events and trends and recommends corrective action.

documentation: Elopement risk assessment in the resident record
Service Plan interventions and any negotiated risk agreement
At-risk resident photograph binder (updated at each reassessment)
Shift check logs
Weekly door alarm test log
Timed missing resident log and incident report
IDPH serious incident report, if applicable
Missing resident drill evaluation (DIS-03)
Administrator event review and QI minutes

policies.category: Safety and Protection
policies.title: Restraints and Restrictive Practices
policies.applies_to: All staff, residents and visiting contractors at [AGENCY NAME], for both assisted living and shared housing.
policies.purpose: To protect each resident's right to freedom from restraint and from restrictive practices, to prevent restraint used for staff convenience, and to set a safe and lawful process for any resident-specific safety measure.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not use physical or chemical restraint, and does not use seclusion, locked confinement or other restrictive practices. Resident rights under Section 95 of the Act and 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.6000 govern a resident's freedom from restraint; the Administrator confirms the exact current rule text at each annual policy review (GOV-01). Restraint will never be used for discipline, staff convenience, or to make up for low staffing. Use of a restraint that harms a resident may be abuse and will be handled under RTS-02. A resident-specific safety measure that is not a restraint, such as a bed rail the resident requests, a door alert or a motion sensor, must be agreed with the resident or representative and documented in a negotiated risk agreement or the service plan (NRA-01, CARE-01). [AGENCY NAME] follows the Americans with Disabilities Act and will not place restrictions on a resident because of disability, and will make reasonable modifications to help a resident stay safely. If a resident's needs cannot be met without restraint, the Administrator will begin the admission or retention review in RES-01, RES-02 and TERM-01, not use restraint.

definitions.definition: Any manual method, device or material attached to or near a resident's body that the resident cannot easily remove and that limits free movement or normal access to the body. Examples include wrist ties, vests, lap trays the resident cannot remove, and tucked sheets that pin a resident.
A medication used to control behavior or restrict movement that is not required to treat a medical condition.
Keeping a resident alone in a room or area from which the resident cannot freely leave.
Any rule or action that limits a resident's freedom, movement, choice or access to people or items, other than one the resident freely chooses.
A device or step the resident or representative understands and agrees to, that the resident can decline or end, and that is documented.

procedures: At orientation and annually, the Administrator trains all staff that restraint and restrictive practices are prohibited, how to recognize them, and how to report them (PER-06).

Staff may not tie, hold, lock in, sedate, or physically limit a resident's movement, except in a genuine emergency, for the shortest time needed, to prevent immediate serious harm. Staff then call 911 and the Administrator immediately.
In any emergency hold, the staff member stays with the resident, watches breathing and skin, and ends the hold as soon as the danger passes.
The charge person records any emergency physical intervention on an incident report before the shift ends, and the Administrator reviews it within one business day.
The Administrator decides whether the event meets the definition of abuse or neglect under RTS-02, and whether IDPH reporting under INC-01 is required.

A resident or representative may ask for a safety measure, such as a bed rail, alarm or lap belt for a wheelchair. The Licensed Nurse assesses the request, including entrapment and injury risks, and explains the risks and less restrictive alternatives to the resident.

If the resident or representative still chooses the measure, the parties sign a negotiated risk agreement or add it to the service plan, with a stated reason, a review date, and a statement that the resident may stop using it at any time.

A safety measure is not used if the resident cannot remove it and has not clearly chosen it, or if it limits movement as a way to manage behavior. In those cases it would be a restraint and is not allowed.
The Licensed Nurse reviews each active safety measure at every reassessment and at any change of condition, and removes it when no longer needed.

Medication is never used to control behavior for staff convenience. Any medication change for behavior must be ordered by the prescriber after evaluation, and the Licensed Nurse reviews it with MED-01 and CARE-05.

For behaviors that put others at risk, staff first use person-centered approaches: finding the cause, reducing noise and triggers, offering activity, and giving one-to-one attention. The approach is written into the service plan.
Doors and exits are not locked in a way that traps residents, and any alarm or delayed-egress system must comply with life safety rules (PP-03, SAF-01).
Staff who see or suspect a restraint or restrictive practice report it at once to the Administrator. Reports may also be made to the Ombudsman or IDPH, and retaliation is prohibited (RTS-02, RTS-04).
Each quarter, the QI Committee reviews all safety measures in use, emergency interventions and related incidents to confirm that no restraint is used (QI-01).
The Administrator compares this policy with the current Section 95 and 295.6000 text at each annual review and updates it as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces the prohibition, reviews all emergency interventions, decides on reporting and trains staff.
Assesses safety measure requests, documents risk discussions and reviews measures at each reassessment.
Never restrain residents, use person-centered approaches, and report any restraint or suspicion at once.
May request, accept, decline or end a safety measure, after the risks are explained.
Audits safety measures and incidents each quarter.

documentation: Staff training roster on restraint prohibition
Incident reports for any emergency physical intervention
Negotiated risk agreements and service plan entries for safety measures
Safety measure assessments and reassessment notes
Administrator review notes and any IDPH or abuse reports
QI minutes reviewing safety measures
Annual policy review record

policies.category: Daily Living
policies.title: Activities and Social Programming
policies.applies_to: All residents of [AGENCY NAME]; activity staff, direct care staff and the Administrator. Dementia program requirements apply wherever [AGENCY NAME] offers a special dementia program.
policies.purpose: To give residents meaningful, voluntary social, physical, cognitive and spiritual activities suited to their interests and abilities, and to meet the cognitive stimulation requirement for dementia programs under 210 ILCS 9/150.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] offers a regular activities program that reflects what residents like and can do. Participation is always voluntary. Activities are planned from information gathered at the pre-admission assessment and reviewed with residents (CARE-01). Where [AGENCY NAME] offers a special dementia program, it will provide cognitive stimulation and activities that fit residents' abilities, and will staff the program appropriately, as 210 ILCS 9/150 requires (C5). Any optional activity that carries a fee, such as outings or special classes, is stated in the establishment contract with its fee (CON-01, CON-02). Participation and resident satisfaction are reviewed in the Quality Improvement program (QI-01).

definitions.definition: A planned or spontaneous event that gives a resident social contact, purposeful engagement, exercise, learning, spiritual connection or enjoyment.
Activity that engages memory, attention, language or reasoning in ways suited to the resident's abilities, for example reminiscence, music, simple crafts, sorting tasks and word games.
An activity or outing that residents may choose to join and that may carry a separate fee stated in the contract.
The staff member [AGENCY NAME] designates to plan, run and document activities.

procedures: At pre-admission assessment, the assessing staff member records the resident's past interests, preferred routines, faith practices, hobbies, language, sensory limits and level of independence. The Activities Coordinator receives this information within three business days of admission.
Within 14 days after move-in, the Activities Coordinator meets with the resident to confirm preferences and records a personal activity profile in the record.

For residents in a dementia program, the profile also describes cognitive abilities, best time of day, helpful cues and activities likely to calm or engage the resident, and is reviewed with the Licensed Nurse (CARE-04).

Each month the Activities Coordinator publishes a calendar covering mornings, afternoons and at least some evenings and weekends. It includes physical, social, cognitive, creative, spiritual and community activities. The calendar is posted in common areas and given to residents who want a copy.
The calendar offers activities at different ability levels, and includes small-group and one-to-one options for residents who prefer not to join groups or cannot leave their rooms.
In a dementia program, the Activities Coordinator schedules cognitive stimulation daily, and direct care staff offer short, informal engagement between scheduled sessions.
Staff invite residents to take part but never require it. A resident who declines is not penalized, and the refusal is respected. Staff try again later with a different approach.
The Administrator reviews staffing so that enough staff are available to help residents attend and take part, including residents who need mobility aid or cueing (PER-01).

Optional activities with a fee are listed with the fee in the contract schedule. Before a resident is charged, the Business Office confirms the resident or representative agreed to the activity and the fee (CON-02).
Outings that need transportation follow DL-02, and staff confirm safe coverage at the site before the outing leaves.
Activity staff use only supplies and equipment that are safe, clean and suited to residents' abilities and cognitive status, and supervise any activity involving sharp, small or hazardous items.

Activity staff record each activity held, the attendance and each resident's response, at least weekly in the activity log, and note any significant change in a resident's mood, interest or abilities for the Licensed Nurse (CARE-05).
The Activities Coordinator asks residents for suggestions at least quarterly, through the resident council, surveys or one-to-one talks, and records changes made in response (RTS-04).
Each quarter, the Activities Coordinator gives the QI Committee participation counts, satisfaction results and the response to any concern, and the committee decides on changes (QI-01).
The Administrator reviews the program annually, including the budget, the dementia program content and staff training, and records the review.

responsibilities.duty: Funds and staffs the program, reviews it annually and ensures it meets dementia program requirements.
Builds activity profiles, plans the calendar, runs and logs activities and reports to QI.
Help residents attend, offer informal engagement and report changes in mood or interest.
Reviews activity needs for residents with cognitive impairment and builds them into the service plan.
Bills optional activity fees only as agreed in the contract.
Reviews participation and satisfaction each quarter.

policies.title: Transportation, Smoking, Visitors and Pets
policies.applies_to: All residents, visitors, essential support persons, volunteers and staff of [AGENCY NAME], including shared housing operations where staff absences for transport can affect safety coverage.
policies.purpose: To set clear, written rules on transportation, smoking, visiting and pets that protect resident safety and rights, and to make sure those rules and any related fees are disclosed in the establishment contract and at admission.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will state its transportation arrangements and fees in the establishment contract (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2030, C8). Smoking rules are written and given to every applicant at admission. Visiting is governed by resident rights and by the essential support person rule (ESP-01, RTS-01); visiting is not restricted except as the resident chooses or as law permits. Pet rules are set by [AGENCY NAME] and are disclosed in the contract. Where [AGENCY NAME] operates a shared housing establishment, at least one staff member must remain on site at all times, so no staff member may leave on transport duty unless that coverage is still in place (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000(k), C7 is referenced in PER-02). In assisted living, at least one staff member must remain awake, on duty and on site at all times (PER-02).

definitions.definition: Rides arranged, scheduled or provided by [AGENCY NAME] staff or contractors, with or without a fee.
A person designated by the resident or representative to provide in-person support, whose access is protected by ESP-01.
An outdoor area identified by [AGENCY NAME], away from entrances and windows, where smoking is allowed if permitted by law and the policy.
A dog (or miniature horse where applicable) individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, treated differently from a pet under the ADA.
An animal kept for companionship that does not meet the service animal definition.

procedures: The Administrator decides what transportation, if any, [AGENCY NAME] offers (for example scheduled outings, medical appointments, shopping), who drives, and the fee. The Governing Body approves the fee schedule.

The Admissions Coordinator lists transportation arrangements and fees in the establishment contract and explains them to the applicant before signing (CON-01, CON-02). Fee changes require 30 days' written notice.

Each driver must hold a valid Illinois driver's license, have a satisfactory driving record check and have completed the Nurse Aide Registry and background check process required by PER-04. Copies are in the employee file.
Before each trip, the driver or Maintenance Director checks the vehicle's condition, seat belts, wheelchair securement equipment and emergency kit, and records the check on the vehicle log.
Staff record each trip: date, driver, residents carried, destination, times out and in. Residents who need help in transit are assigned a staff escort.

Before any staff member leaves the building on transport duty, the charge person confirms that the staffing required by PER-01 and PER-02 stays in place. In shared housing, at least one staff member remains on site at all times; in assisted living, at least one remains awake, on duty and on site, and CPR-certified direct care coverage is not interrupted.
If safe coverage cannot be arranged, the trip is postponed or an additional qualified staff member is called in, and the Administrator is notified.

Smoking: the Administrator adopts a written smoking policy that complies with Illinois and local law, states where smoking is or is not allowed, and describes fire-safety measures such as ashtrays, lighters and oxygen safety (PP-03). The Admissions Coordinator gives the policy to every applicant at admission, and the resident signs that he or she received it.

Staff do not allow smoking near oxygen or in any place not designated. The Licensed Nurse assesses any resident who smokes for fire risk and safe-smoking needs and records them in the service plan or a negotiated risk agreement (NRA-01).

Visitors: [AGENCY NAME] posts visiting hours for general visitors as [VISITING HOURS], but a resident's essential support persons have access as stated in ESP-01, and no resident's right to receive visitors of his or her choice is limited without the resident's consent or lawful reason (RTS-01).

Visitors sign in at the front desk. Staff may ask a visitor to leave only if the visitor is disruptive, a threat to residents, or the resident asks him or her to go, and the Administrator records the reason. Reports of suspected abuse by a visitor go through RTS-02.
Visitors with signs of contagious illness are asked to postpone visits or follow infection control rules in CARE-03.

Pets: the Administrator writes a pet policy covering allowed species, number, size, vaccination and licensing proof, resident responsibility for care, cost of damage, and what happens if a pet cannot be cared for. The policy is disclosed in the contract (CON-01).
Service animals are allowed according to ADA requirements and are not treated as pets. Staff may ask only the two questions the ADA allows, and may remove an animal only for reasons the ADA permits.
The Administrator reviews transportation, smoking, visitor and pet complaints and incidents each quarter, and reports trends to the QI Committee (QI-01).

responsibilities.duty: Approves transportation fees and the smoking, visitor and pet rules.

Confirms safe coverage before a staff member leaves for transport, and enforces smoking and visiting rules on shift.
Hold required licenses and clearances, inspect vehicles and log trips.
Assesses residents who smoke and writes safety measures.
